item.content:encoded:
With Helion’s release last year, it aimed at enabling developers to write GPU kernels in PyTorch-native Python and let its powerful autotuner do the work that used to require hand-written Triton and abstract away hardware-specific implementation details. Helion’s autotuner explores thousands of kernel configurations and routinely lands within a few percent of expert-tuned code, and oftentimes exceeding it.

The question that now needs to be answered is this: If a kernel has already been autotuned and optimized to the best of a developer’s ability, is there anything left?

There is. It lives below the kernel, in the compiler.

Every kernel autotuner in the ecosystem whether it is Helion’s, Triton’s, the one inside torch.compile, they all search the same thing: tile shapes, warp counts, pipeline stages, memory access strategy. All of those are decisions about what work each thread block does. Underneath them sits a second set of decisions about how that work becomes machine assembly instructions generated by ptxas, NVIDIA’s PTX assembler. Things like register allocation policy, fine-grained instruction scheduling, code-generation heuristics are left at their defaults for all kernels shipping today – not because the defaults are optimal, but because nothing was searching and optimizing them!

Helion now enables this, and this post is about what that second compiler-specific space contains, why searching it jointly with the kernel configuration space shows further improvements on kernels that were already deemed to be optimal.

The searching is done by NVIDIA’s CompileIQ, which optimizes ptxas controls the way an autotuner optimizes tile sizes and packages the result as a portable Advanced Control File (ACF). Most users won’t run that search themselves: CompileIQ publishes pre-tuned ACF catalogs that Helion’s autotuner can now evaluate alongside the kernel configurations it already explores.

Starting off with highly-optimized kernels & optimizing the last-mile

It matters a great deal what baseline one compares against. A “we made kernels faster” claim is easy if the starting point is a naive kernel, and close to meaningless for real-world workloads.

The kernels we use here come from the pretuned_kernels/ in the Helion repository, roughly 27 kernels covering the shapes that show up in real model code: FP8 and NVFP4 quantization, RMSNorm variants, RoPE, grouped GEMM, causal depthwise convolution, Gated DeltaNet decode, and fused model regions like a Qwen3 decode layer.

The important property to note here is that these are not autotuned on the fly. Each one ships with ahead-of-time heuristic files per architecture: _helion_aot_rms_norm_cuda_sm90.py for H100, _helion_aot_rms_norm_cuda_sm100.py for B200 etc. that Helion selects at runtime. The autotuning search already happened offline, and its result is baked in. When this program is run, the user gets tuned performance with no search cost.

That is our baseline: a kernel whose configuration space has already been swept, on the hardware it’s running on, by the kernel authors and the Helion compiler developers. If there’s headroom below that, it’s real headroom and that’s the last-mile focus of this post.

What Helion’s autotuner searches, and where it stops

A Helion kernel is ordinary PyTorch with one new idea – tiles:

import torch, helion, helion.language as hl

@helion.kernel()
def softmax(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    n, _m = x.size()
    out = torch.empty_like(x)
    for tile_n in hl.tile(n):
        out[tile_n, :] = torch.nn.functional.softmax(x[tile_n, :], dim=1)
    return out

The user never says how big a tile is. That’s the point: hl.tile declares that the iteration space is tiled, and the autotuner decides the rest. A single kernel definition implicitly generates a search space of thousands of Triton configurations that span block_sizes, loop_orders, l2_grouping, num_warps, num_stages, indexing (pointer arithmetic vs. block pointers vs. TMA descriptors), pid_type, reduction_loops, and more. Helion lowers through TorchInductor to Triton, compiles each candidate, times it, and keeps the winner.

Then the winning Triton kernel goes to ptxas, and everything from that point down happens at PTXAS’ default settings. The kernel autotuner’s search space is defined by what the kernel language can express, and no kernel language expresses “allocate registers differently”. This compiler control surface is a separate interface, exposed by ptxas itself starting from CUDA 13.3.

It is imperative to mention that this exploration is genuinely hard. There are complex interactions between various compiler controls: a change to register allocation shifts occupancy, which changes whether a scheduling decision helps or hurts. The right setting is workload-specific, and there’s no universal answer to publish. And the payoff per unit of human effort is poor, which is exactly the profile of a problem one hands off to a search algorithm.

The joint search: Helion Autotuner and PTXAS’ Advanced Controls

Helion exposes the underlying compiler control space through two settings. Controls are packaged in an Advanced Control File (ACF, typically ending with .acf) which is a binary artifact applied at compile time, portable and versionable, that users can ship alongside their kernel.

The first setting pins a known-good ACF as part of a config the user has already chosen:

softmax_tuned = helion.kernel(
    config=helion.Config(
        advanced_controls_file="h100_example1.acf",
        block_sizes=[4],
        num_warps=8,
        num_stages=2,
        reduction_loops=[512],
        indexing=["pointer", "pointer", "tensor_descriptor",
        "tensor_descriptor", "pointer", "pointer"],
    ),
    static_shapes=True,
)(_softmax)

The second is a more interesting case. It hands a list of ACFs to Helion’s own autotuner and lets them be searched as just another dimension, alongside tile sizes and warp counts:

softmax_search = helion.kernel(
    autotune_search_acf=[
        "acfs/helion-booster-pack/candidate_03.acf",
        "acfs/helion-booster-pack/candidate_11.acf",
        "acfs/helion-booster-pack/candidate_17.acf",
    ],
    autotune_compile_timeout=120,
    static_shapes=True,
)(_softmax)

Two things are worth pointing out in this mode:

  • The empty string is appended for you. Helion automatically adds “”, meaning “no ACF, compiler defaults”, to the list that is supplied. The default configuration is therefore always a candidate in the search, and the autotuner will only select an ACF if it actually won on measured time. The worst case of turning this on is that you spend some autotuning budget and get back the kernel you already had. That property is what makes it tempting to try on a kernel you care about.
  • Sequential tuning finds a local optimum; this joint method doesn’t. This is the substantive argument for doing it in one loop rather than two. Suppose you autotune the kernel first, get block_sizes=[128, 128] with num_stages=4, and then go searching for compiler controls. You are now searching the control space conditioned on a kernel config that was itself chosen under default controls. But those dimensions are coupled through the hardware: block size and stage count determine register pressure and shared-memory footprint, and register allocation policy is precisely what decides whether that pressure causes spills. A control set that would shine at block_sizes=[64, 64] never gets evaluated there, because the kernel config was frozen before the compiler search began.The reverse ordering has the same problem. Searching both together is the only ordering that doesn’t have it, which is why autotune_search_acf lives inside Helion’s autotuner rather than being a post-processing step.

The cost is search time. Each ACF multiplies the number of compile-and-measure trials, so this is not something to leave on by default for every kernel in a codebase. It is something to run once, offline, on a kernel that matters, and then pin the result with advanced_controls_file, exactly the way autotuned configs are pinned today.

Where do these Advanced Control Files come from

Now that we’ve understood the benefits of joint autotuning of Helion parameters with PTXAS’ advanced control files (ACF), the natural question one may have is how can these ACFs be generated. That is where NVIDIA’s CompileIQ comes into the picture.

CompileIQ treats compiler-control selection as a hyperparameter optimization problem. It pulls a curated search space for the target compiler and toolkit version, then runs an evolutionary search: propose a population of candidate control sets, compile each one, check correctness against a reference, time the survivors, breed the winners, repeat. The output of this search process is an ACF file. There is nothing GPU-specific about the search algorithm itself, and the only GPU-specific parts are what is entirely in the objective function that the user writes, which is usually a few lines around triton.testing.do_bench.

For most users however, the additional search budget is unnecessary, because the searching has been done. CompileIQ publishes Booster Packs – pre-tuned ACF catalogs – on its GitHub releases. The current helion-booster-pack contains 24 ACFs tuned across a range of Helion kernels, validated against ptxas from CUDA 13.4, targeting B200. So the realistic workflow for users is: download the pack, point Helion’s autotune_search_acf at it, autotune once, pin what wins. No search space to design, no objective function to write, no compiler expertise required!

If you have a workload the pack doesn’t cover, pip install compileiq and run your own targeted search. That path is documented in NVIDIA’s CompileIQ blog post and in various CompileIQ examples.

Helion and CompileIQ: Experimental Results

This section highlights many possible ways in which one can run a CompileIQ optimization campaign on Helion kernels. As a sample case study we applied CompileIQ to the pretuned nvfp4_gemv_fp4in_kernel, a Helion W4A4 (NVFP4 weight x NVFP4 activation) decode GEMV kernel that already ships a checked-in Helion AOT config for its target shape. The question: is there performance CompileIQ can extract below Helion’s own autotuning layer ,i.e., at the ptxas compilation stage?

Environment and Methodology

Benchmarking was conducted on a GB200 system with sm_100 (Blackwell, compute capability 10.0), utilizing ptxas 13.3.73 (CUDA 13.3), CompileIQ 1.0.3, Triton 3.8.0, and an editable source installation of Helion. All timing evaluations were executed via triton.testing.do_bench with the GPU clock locked. Every observed performance improvement was re-measured independently, validated against the PyTorch reference implementation for numerical correctness, and statistically filtered using a Welch’s t-test (p < 0.05) alongside Cohen’s d (d > 0.2). Complete statistical metrics are provided alongside each result below.

Kernel Description

nvfp4_gemv_fp4in_kernel in helion/pretuned_kernels/nvfp4_gemv/nvfp4_gemv.py, computing out = (weight @ x) * alpha for a decode (one output row) GEMV. Both the packed NVFP4 weight and activation bytes are unpacked per K-group via hl.load_float4_e2m1fn_x16_to_float16, accumulated in fp16 over a 16-way static range, and scaled by a decoded E4M3 block scaler.

This kernel includes a checked-in AOT configuration specifically for the N=8192, K=28672 “down_proj” decode-GEMV shape in _helion_aot_nvfp4_gemv_cuda_sm100.py:

_CONFIG_FP4IN_DEFAULT = {
    "block_sizes": [4, 256],
    "num_warps": 2,
    "num_stages": 3,
    "range_multi_buffers": [None, True],
}

Using Runtime as CompileIQ Objective Function

Using runtime as the CompileIQ objective function lets us optimize execution speed directly. The objective function takes a candidate ACF configuration, applies it to our fixed Helion kernel, and evaluates it: the kernel runs once, its output is checked against the PyTorch reference implementation, and only configurations that pass correctness are then benchmarked with triton.testing.do_bench. Any configuration that fails correctness returns an invalid score and is dropped from the search before it ever contributes a timing measurement.

def objective(config) -> float:
    acf_path = ... # write `config` to a .acf, or None for baseline
    kernel = _make_kernel(acf_path)
    got = run()
    _check(got, ref, "fp4in", N, K) # correctness gate
    return do_bench(run, warmup=25, rep=100, return_mode="mean")

We initialize a Search instance that couples our scoring routine to an evolutionary autotuner over PTXAS compiler controls, then invoke .start(). It sweeps candidate ACFs across generations generations of a pool_size-sized population, breeding the top-performing control configurations forward into each subsequent iteration.

config = SearchConfiguration(problem_type="min", generations=8, pool_size=15)
tuner = Search(
    objective_function=objective,
    search_space=PtxasSearchSpace(version=cuda_version, variant="default"),
    search_config=config,
    dump_results="nvfp4_gemv_results.csv",
    worker_type=WorkerTypes.ISOLATED, # crashing ACF candidates shouldn't kill the search
)

with gpu_benchmark_mode(clock_mhz=target_clock_mhz, raise_on_failure=False):
    results = tuner.start(task_timeout=60)

Executing an evolutionary search with CompileIQ across PTXAS ACFs, spanning 8 generations with a pool size of 15 candidates over our fixed Helion configuration on GB200 yielded an optimized ACF control set. This candidate reduced execution time from a baseline of 0.0971 ms down to 0.0928 ms, delivering a 1.047x (4.7%) speedup as measured directly within the search’s scoring loop.

sample baseline run: 0.09713 ms
Best runtime (CompileIQ Search): 0.0928 ms
Speedup: 1.047x

Validation of CompileIQ Search Results

To confirm our findings, every speedup is re-measured independently using increased warmup and repetition iterations under fixed GPU clock frequencies. Each configuration undergoes strict correctness verification against the reference model alongside a Welch’s t-test and Cohen’s d filter. This serves as our rigorous statistical threshold (requiring p < 0.05, cohens_d > 0.2, and optimized.mean < baseline.mean) to verify performance gains before trusting the numbers.

# run 1
baseline:  n=1744 mean=0.09752ms std=0.00218
optimized: n=2018 mean=0.09301ms std=0.00133
speedup_mean:   1.0485
p_value:  0.0
cohens_d: 2.501
significant: True

# run 2 (independent re-run)
baseline:  n=1757 mean=0.09744ms std=0.00216
optimized: n=2028 mean=0.09299ms std=0.00130
speedup_mean:   1.0478
p_value:  0.0
cohens_d: 2.489
significant: True

The two executions remain virtually identical within experimental variance: with d ≈ 2.5 demonstrating a massive effect size that easily surpasses our statistical threshold of 0.2 , verifying that this ACF performance gain is genuine.

The two runs are virtually identical within experimental variance, and d ≈ 2.5 in both is a massive effect size nearly 12.5x past our d > 0.2 gate, confirming this ACF performance gain is genuine, not noise.

Tuning against a hardware metric instead of runtime

While execution speed is a common optimization goal, CompileIQ is not limited to runtime alone. Integrating directly with Nsight Compute (ncu) enables the objective function to target any hardware metric exposed by the tool. To determine the key architectural bottleneck limiting kernel performance, we start by evaluating its profile and analyzing nvfp4_gemv_fp4in_kernel on a GB200 system highlights the following bottlenecks:

Section: GPU Speed of Light Throughput
Memory Throughput               %       78.99
L1/TEX Cache Throughput         %       89.35
Compute (SM) Throughput         %       37.29

Section: Occupancy
Theoretical Occupancy                   %    25.0
Achieved Occupancy                      %    21.63

  Est. Speedup: 21.01%
  ... theoretical occupancy (25.0%) is limited by the number of required
  registers.

Profiling shows the kernel is register-limited. NCU’s own cost model attributes a 21% ‘Est. Speedup’ opportunity to occupancy, and this ceiling is set by register count, something PTXAS’s register-allocation controls can directly influence.

Switching the objective from runtime to occupancy only touches two things: what the objective function scores, and the search’s problem_type:

# objective(): do_bench(...) becomes an ncu metric read
return _measure_occupancy(acf_path) # ncu: sm__warps_active.avg.pct_of_peak_sustained_active

# search config: minimize runtime -> maximize occupancy
config = SearchConfiguration(problem_type="max", generations=4, pool_size=6)

Pointing the search at achieved occupancy itself across 4 generations × pool size 6, rather than runtime, found a candidate that moved the proxy metric by +0.16pp (21.60% → 21.76% achieved occupancy, p = 9.2e-23, d = 13.17) and, independently re-measured, translated into a modest but statistically solid runtime win of ~1.75-2.0% (p = 3.6e-116, d = 0.78).

Multi-Objective Tuning

CompileIQ can also perform multi-objective tuning, where the scoring routine evaluates candidates along multiple dimensions simultaneously by returning a tuple rather than a scalar float. Instead of isolating a single top performer, the autotuning process maps out candidates along the Pareto frontier, identifying control sets that are not dominated across all target metrics. This yields a unified ACF optimized jointly for execution runtime alongside L1TEX cache throughput.

def objective(config) -> tuple[float, float]:
    runtime_ms = do_bench(run, warmup=25, rep=100, return_mode="mean")
    l1_throughput = _measure_l1throughput(acf_path)
    return runtime_ms, -l1_throughput

8 generations × pool size 15 converged to a single dominant candidate on the Pareto front. Unlike a tradeoff curve, this single point beats every other evaluated candidate on both axes simultaneously in the search’s own scoring. Validating it on a fresh cache at shipping-grade trial counts:

=== RUNTIME (ms, lower is better) ===
p_value=3.516e-295  cohens_d=87.024
speedup_mean=1.0689x
=== L1TEX THROUGHPUT (%, higher is better; internally negated) ===
p_value=7.123e-19  cohens_d=3.686
baseline L1TEX THROUGHPUT mean=81.5087%
candidate L1TEX THROUGHPUT mean=85.9620%

Multi-objective tuning found an ACF delivering a validated 6.9% runtime speedup, accompanied by a simultaneous 4.5pp L1TEX throughput gain (81.51% → 85.96%). Both results are statistically significant (p ≪ 0.05, Cohen’s d ≫ 0.2), with neither metric being traded off against the other.

Joint ACF Optimization Across Multiple Input Shapes

While earlier evaluations focused on a single kernel shape, N=8192, K=28672, real-world model deployment demands coverage across multiple configurations. The nvfp4_gemv implementation ships with several pre-tuned Helion AOT configurations, including a dedicated setup for N=15360, K=5120. Instead of maintaining distinct control files per shape, CompileIQ enables a unified search to discover a single, joint ACF that maximizes performance across both shapes simultaneously.

def objective(config) -> tuple[float, ...]:
    """One shared ACF, one runtime score per shape (both minimize)."""
    acf_path = ... # write `config` to a temp .acf, or None for baseline
    return tuple(_bench_shape(acf_path, shape) for shape in SHAPES)

Executing an 8-generation search with a pool size of 15 across both shapes yielded a Pareto front containing 4 optimal candidates:

Candidate down_proj 15360_5120
pareto_0 0.0927 ms 0.0309 ms
pareto_1 0.0927 ms 0.0309 ms
pareto_2 0.0944 ms 0.0308 ms
pareto_3 0.0917 ms 0.0321 ms

Compared to the default benchmark times of 0.0972 ms for down_proj and 0.0315 ms for 15360_5120, pareto_0 emerges as the standout configuration that consistently outpaces the baseline across both target tensor dimensions.

To confirm these performance gains, we execute an independent validation of pareto_0 on each individual shape. Both configurations comfortably pass our statistical validation (1.05x speedup with a p-value of 1.1e-224 and Cohen’s d of 67.71 for down_proj, and 1.01x speedup with a p-value of 6.2e-73 and a d of 4.54 on the 15360_5120 shape), far exceeding our benchmark requirements and proving these gains represent genuine performance improvements rather than system noise. A single joint ACF successfully outperforms the default baseline across both target dimensions simultaneously.

Applicability of this workflow for end-to-end model tuning

While the focus of this entire post is about optimizing the underlying compiler for extracting more performance from individual kernels, it is important to zoom out and highlight how a workflow like this could be utilized for end-to-end tuning of models on PyTorch.

The first step is to profile and characterize the most important kernels that are part of the model which you wish to optimize. Then, each of these kernels can then be a target of CompileIQ optimization, with an associated Advanced Control File to extract maximum performance from that instantiation of the kernel. These get applied during runtime using Helion’s pinned autotune configurations, using Triton’s ptxas_options API or directly via the PTXAS command line depending on the entry point of each kernel’s implementation.

We want to be upfront about the expected gains: On kernels that are already highly optimized, compiler-control tuning has shown runtime improvements on the order of 2-7% which may still mean a lot for critical kernels in top models. Less optimized kernels have achieved double-digit performance gains, offering greater potential for meaningful end-to-end improvements.

The important points to note are that it is found automatically, and requires little to no compiler expertise, it is verified against your own correctness check, and the result is a file you can commit next to the kernel and reapply on every build. It is the difference between a few percent that exists in principle and a few percent you actually ship.

It also compounds exactly where you’d want it to. There are high-value kernels inside inference loops that run continuously across large fleets. Even a few percent at the bottom of the stack, applied to the operations that dominate a decode step, is valuable at that scale.

Caveats

  • ACFs are hardware- and toolkit-specific: An ACF tuned for sm_90 is not valid on sm_100. Applying a mismatched ACF can produce incorrect results or runtime errors, not just slower code. The booster pack manifest states its target architecture and toolkit version. This is also why the correctness check in the search loop is not optional.
  • Search-time is a nontrivial cost: Every ACF in autotune_search_acf multiplies your autotuning trials. Use it offline on kernels that matter, then pin the winner.
  • Gains are workload-specific: The result depends on the workload, the shapes, the architecture, and how much headroom the kernel has left. The only number that matters for your kernel is the one you measure on your kernel.

Your turn to try this out!

If you’ve never written a GPU kernel: start at pretuned_kernels/. Pick something close to what you need, read it and then run it. The kernels are short, and they run at tuned speed immediately, with no autotuning wait.

If you already use Helion: download the helion-booster-pack, add autotune_search_acf=[…] to one kernel you care about, and autotune it. The no-ACF baseline stays in the search, so the downside is bounded at the time you spend. See Helion’s examples/acfs/ for a worked example.

If you work on kernels for a living: the takeaway here is not the tool itself. It is that the compiler’s control surface is a legitimate optimization space, it is searchable, and most people are not yet searching it. That is true of any compiler that exposes tunable controls, on any backend. We’re hopeful that we’ve inspired you to explore this space!

Licensing

Helion is open source and hosted by the PyTorch Foundation. CompileIQ is free to use and it is distributed under the NVIDIA Software License Agreement, a proprietary EULA. The ACF files it produces are freely distributable, which is why booster packs can be published and why an ACF can be committed alongside a kernel in an open repository.

item.content:encoded:
Frontier models span language, video and audio, on architectures from dense and mixture-of-experts transformers to diffusion, state-space, world and structure-prediction models. PyTorch is where AI research happens, where the models are defined, and increasingly where production happens too. Researchers want to experiment and innovate, and customers want the performance AWS Trainium offers to enable them to achieve their performance and scale goals. The training and serving libraries are written against PyTorch’s own APIs, and new libraries and new versions ship continuously. Over the last several years, PyTorch made those APIs accelerator-agnostic, with official extension points for registering custom hardware.

Today, to address the growing demand from the developers and research community on Trainium, we are excited to share an even simpler approach to program the chip as a standard PyTorch device, ahead of its open source launch at PyTorch Conference North America on Oct. 20. AWS Trainium is a portfolio of AI chips designed from the ground up for next generation cloud scale AI training and inference. We are announcing TorchNeuron, an open source native PyTorch backend for Trainium, so the model code, the libraries, and the tools you already use run on Trainium. This integration builds directly on the accelerator-agnostic extension points, including the PrivateUse1 device backend and torch.accelerator APIs, created by the PyTorch community.

TorchNeuron supports eager execution for research and debugging including new adaptive eager mode with improved performance, torch.compile for production performance, and the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) for custom kernels, on Trainium2 and Trainium3. Also, with Neuron Explorer, performance engineers use the same torch.profiler to trace execution from framework to hardware, linking every event back to its source line to pinpoint bottlenecks and optimize efficiently. TorchNeuron will be released as open source under Apache 2.0 at github.com/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx, going live as public Beta on Oct. 20.

“PyTorch’s vision is straightforward: developers should have a consistent experience across hardware platforms. Native support for AWS Trainium expands that choice, enabling researchers and engineers to experiment and iterate using the eager execution and distributed APIs they already know. Teams can take advantage of Trainium’s capabilities without reinventing their workflows or leaving the PyTorch ecosystem.” – Jana van Greunen, Director of PyTorch Engineering at Meta

Getting started: Easy device switching

Getting started is straightforward. Run your code on Trainium using the pointer: .to('neuron').

# Run a training loop on Trainium
model = MyModel().to('neuron')   # the only change
optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters())
for batch in dataloader:
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss = criterion(model(batch), targets)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

Modern code written against torch.accelerator, PyTorch’s recommended device-agnostic API, runs unmodified. A compiled model needs the Neuron backend named, once with torch.compiler.set_default_backend("neuron"), after which torch.compile(model) takes it, or per call as torch.compile(model, backend="neuron").

# Run a compiled training loop on Trainium
torch.compiler.set_default_backend("neuron")  # call once, before any compile
model = MyModel().to('neuron')
model.compile()  # no backend argument
optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters())

for batch in dataloader:
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss = criterion(model(batch), targets)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

Capabilities

TorchNeuron registers Trainium through PrivateUse1, PyTorch’s official extension point for custom hardware, so the standard APIs work as written: torch.nn, torch.tensor, torch.autocast, torch.distributed, and torch.profiler all operate on the neuron device. The two execution modes of PyTorch, eager and torch.compile work natively.

High-level architecture diagram of TorchNeuron (details).

Eager

Eager runs operations immediately, so Python control flow, prints, and breakpoints all work with no compile or trace step. This is the mode for research and debugging. Eager mode dispatches operations individually. Executed directly, each operation compiles its own Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) file, launches it on device, and moves its intermediates through HBM. We are also introducing adaptive eager mode (experimental), to reduce the launch cost and provide better opportunities to fuse operations to approach performance of compiled graph without a code change, while retaining the interactive experience.

torch.compile

torch.compile(model, backend="neuron") captures the model into a graph the Neuron compiler optimizes, and is the mode for stable, high-performance models moving to production. torch.compile can be used to optimize the whole or part of the model and works seamlessly with eager mode. FlexAttention is supported natively. TorchDynamo captures the model into an FX graph, AOTAutograd traces the backward graph ahead of time, the Neuron backend lowers the result, by way of Torch-MLIR, into StableHLO, and the Neuron compiler produces a NEFF file that executes on hardware.

The Neuron inference stacks are built on the same torch.compile support in TorchNeuron. vLLM Neuron is a plugin to vLLM and serves LLMs; vLLM Omni Neuron is a plugin to vLLM Omni and serves diffusion models for image and video generation.

Ops and dtypes

Broad aten operator coverage for ops seen across text, multimodal and vision language, image and video generation and understanding, state space models, and world models. Models can use BF16, FP32, and FP16, with integer and boolean types, and torch.autocast and mixed precision code operate as written. TorchAO and FP8 are currently supported under private Beta and will be made generally available in the next release.

Distributed APIs

Distributed inference and training can use the standard PyTorch APIs and the high-level parallelism modules compose with your model as written: DDP, FSDP2, SimpleFSDP, tensor parallelism, and pipeline parallelism, along with common compositions like FSDP2 with tensor parallelism, ZeRO that are essential for training large models. DTensor and DeviceMesh are supported to handle sharding and the multi-dimensional process groups. The collective APIs (example: all_gather, reduce_scatter, all_reduce) and the P2P APIs (send, recv) are supported. Collectives execute over Trainium’s dedicated collective cores intra-node and over the Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) inter-node, so the communication transport is native to the hardware with no change to PyTorch APIs.

Streams and Events

Torch streams and events are supported natively. torch_neuronx.Stream and torch_neuronx.Event map PyTorch’s stream semantics onto Trainium’s hardware queues. Within a stream, data movement and computation stay in order automatically. Separate streams carry no implicit dependency on one another, so across streams you make that ordering explicit by recording an event on the producing stream and waiting for it on the consuming stream before using the result. The device-agnostic torch.Stream, torch.Event, and torch.accelerator entry points reach the same implementation, so code written against them runs unmodified. An error surfaces at the next synchronization point rather than at the operation that caused it; TorchNeuron tracks the earliest exception and re-raises it there with its original context. In execution, non-default streams multiplex onto a single hardware queue, so they keep ordering, priority, and event semantics but do not each get a dedicated engine; and when host collectives are disabled, a collective issued on a non-default stream keeps its place in that stream’s execution order but runs on the default hardware queue.

Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI)

The Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) lets researchers and developers develop, optimize, and execute custom operators for both eager and torch.compile. Researchers can prototype ideas that require low level hardware control, including new model architectures. Developers can obtain finer performance control beyond Adaptive Eager and torch.compile by calling performance critical NKI kernels directly in model code to replace sequences of standard PyTorch operations (ATen ops).

TorchNeuron also provides Trainium optimized, high-performance operators implemented with NKI and released open source as NKI-lib, covering mainstream LLM and multimodal scenarios for both dense and MoE models, such as FlashAttention and MoE blockwise kernels, which developers can use to improve performance on Trainium. The following example defines and registers a custom NKI operator using the PyTorch recommended register_autograd style:

import torch
import nki
import nki.language as nl
from torch_neuronx import nki_op

# Declaring and implementing NKI kernels
# Note in NKI kernels, the output tensor should be defined as parameter to the kernel
@nki.jit
def sin_kernel(in_ptr0, out_ptr):
    input_tile = nl.load(in_ptr0[0:128])
    output_tile = nl.sin(input_tile)
    nl.store(out_ptr[0:128], value=output_tile)
    return out_ptr

# defining cos since it will be used in backward path of sin
@nki.jit
def cos_kernel(in_ptr0, out_ptr):
    input_tile = nl.load(in_ptr0[0:128])
    output_tile = nl.cos(input_tile)
    nl.store(out_ptr[0:128], value=output_tile)
    return out_ptr

# after this line, there is no NKI code, just native PyTorch, registering custom ops
@nki_op("mylib::pt_nki_sin", mutates_args={})
def pt_nki_sin(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    out = torch.empty_like(x)
    sin_kernel(x, out)
    return out

@nki_op("mylib::pt_nki_cos", mutates_args={})
def pt_nki_cos(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    out = torch.empty_like(x)
    cos_kernel(x, out)
    return out

def pt_nki_sin_backward(ctx, grad):
    x, = ctx.saved_tensors
    return grad * pt_nki_cos(x)  # cos is derivative of sin

def pt_sin_setup_context(ctx, inputs, output):
    x, = inputs
    ctx.save_for_backward(x)

# Register backward pass and context function used during autograd for nki_sin
pt_nki_sin.register_autograd(pt_nki_sin_backward, setup_context=pt_sin_setup_context)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    x = torch.randn(128, 1, device="neuron", requires_grad=True)
    # Forward pass uses sin_kernel
    y = pt_nki_sin(x)
    # Backward pass, autograd calls uses nki_sin_backward() -> cos_kernel()
    loss = y.sum()
    loss.backward()

Profiling with TorchNeuron

TorchNeuron integrates with the standard torch.profiler.profile API extended with a NeuronConfig object that controls Neuron-specific data collection. This allows users to capture and correlate traces from framework-level CPU operations (PyTorch dispatch, Python stacks) as well as Neuron runtime and Trainium activity (controlled by NeuronConfig) enabling end to end performance analysis.

Profiles captured can be visualized in the Neuron Explorer UI, where users can trace execution across framework, runtime, and device, jump from any event to the exact source line (source code viewer), navigate the workload through its call hierarchy (hierarchy viewer), and follow dependency chains to see what each stall is waiting on (dependency chain viewer).

Neuron Explorer also emits a Parquet output with per-op and per-engine metrics, so the same data behind the UI can be queried directly or consumed by agents for automated bottleneck analysis. For programmatic access, users can work with the built-in torch.profiler tools. For example, the key_averages table lets users drill down into specific ops and use the sort_by argument to surface the device-side cost of each op, which is useful for identifying hotspots.

Following code snippet shows an example (details):

import torch
from torch.profiler import profile, ProfilerActivity
from torch_neuronx.profiling import NeuronConfig, ProfileMode, NeuronProfiler

# Configure Neuron profiling and pass appropriate path as OUTPUT_DIR
nc = NeuronConfig(
   modes=[ProfileMode.DEVICE, ProfileMode.RUNTIME],
   profile_output_dir=OUTPUT_DIR,
   capture_enabled_for_nc='0',
   correlate_device_time=True,
)
# NeuronProfiler.export_trace() places the framework trace
# in the same directory as Neuron system traces
exporter = NeuronProfiler(nc)

device = torch.device('neuron')

x = torch.randn(4, 512, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=device)
weight = torch.ones(512, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=device)

def rms_norm_fn(t):
    x_sq = t * t
    mean_sq = x_sq.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
    rms = torch.rsqrt(mean_sq + 1e-6)
    return t * rms * weight

# Profile your workload
with torch.profiler.profile(
    activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU, ProfilerActivity.PrivateUse1],
    experimental_config=nc,
    record_shapes=False,
    on_trace_ready=exporter.export_trace,
    schedule=torch.profiler.schedule(wait=2, warmup=1, active=1),
) as prof:
    for step in range(4):
        with torch.no_grad():
            _ = rms_norm_fn(x)
        torch.neuron.synchronize()
        prof.step()

# Print the per-op summary, sorted by device time to surface hotspots
print(prof.key_averages().table(sort_by="self_privateuse1_time_total", row_limit=4))

For additional capabilities and features refer to Neuron Explorer documentation.

Customers and partners building on TorchNeuron

TorchNeuron is already in use across startups, enterprises, ML industry partners, and academic institutions: spanning autonomous vehicles, robotics, video generation, speech, telecommunications, healthcare, and geospatial modeling. Below is a snapshot of what teams are building today.

“Cartesia is building intelligence that learns from and interacts with the world the way humans do, starting with conversation. Our pioneering work on state-space architectures like Mamba powers Sonic (text-to-speech) and Ink (speech-to-text), the voice AI models behind conversational experiences that feel truly human. Real conversation demands three things at once: quality (naturalness and accuracy), efficiency (low latency at scale), and steerability. Most solutions deliver one or two. We designed our research and products from first principles to deliver all three, which means we need infrastructure that lets us squeeze maximum performance out of every layer without rewriting our stack. With PyTorch native support on AWS Trainium, we ran our standard inference pipeline with minimal changes to our PyTorch code. Small, fast ops map efficiently through the native path, so we didn’t have to hand-write kernels for them. That lets our team concentrate on writing high-performance NKI kernels for the layers that are called repeatedly and drive end-to-end latency. For real-time voice, every millisecond of network distance matters. Running on Trainium gives helps to put Sonic and Ink close to our customers globally.”

Arjun Desai, Cofounder, Cartesia

“Voice is becoming a first-class modality for AI, and Deepgram processes quadrillions of audio tokens a year for more than 200,000 developers and 1,400 organizations. To meet that demand, we need to scale efficiently while continuing to ship better models. Over a multi-month engagement, the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center helped us port our model to PyTorch Native on AWS Trainium. In the benchmarks we evaluated, Trainium processes about 60% more input audio seconds per dollar than our existing GPU baselines, which helps us bring better models to customers at lower prices. We look forward to supporting future AWS AI chips in our solution.”

Adam Sypniewski, CTO, Deepgram

“Hugging Face is the leading open platform for AI builders, providing free access to over 6 million open models, datasets and applications through PyTorch-powered open-source libraries including Transformers and Diffusers. Until now, taking advantage of AWS Trainium required adapting Hugging Face models with Neuron-specific software and configuration; TorchNeuron makes Trainium a native backend for Transformers and Diffusers, so developers can use familiar model definitions through a fully open-source stack – a practical expression of our commitment to silicon neutrality and compatibility. It’s now easier than ever to deploy state-of-the-art open LLMs and the latest open image and video generation models on AWS Trainium, with TRL enabling fine-tuning and reinforcement learning and Neuron kernels delivering optimized performance automatically through our libraries.”

Jeff Boudier, VP Product, Hugging Face

Beyond these customers, we have been working with a number of partners who are building with TorchNeuron to enhance the Trainium ecosystem. These partners include Anyscale, Decart, Kernelize, Loka, Luminal, Makora, Modular, Nota AI, Radix, Wafer, and Yasp.

How TorchNeuron Enables broader compatibility

One of our goals with native PyTorch support is to enable developers to leverage the performance and cost benefits of Trainium while continuing to use the models, libraries, and workflows they already know. This helps preserve their investment in PyTorch, including their model code, inference and training infrastructure, debugging practices, and the community projects they build upon.

The cost of running AI workloads includes the engineering time needed to get them working, optimize their performance, and maintain them as models and libraries evolve. We want developers to spend more time experimenting with architectures and improving model quality, and less time adapting their software to the underlying hardware. They should be able to start with a familiar model or training recipe, adapt it to their workload, and run it on Trainium with minimal changes specific to Neuron.

TorchNeuron provides the foundation for this experience through compatibility with the broader PyTorch. Developers can use libraries such as TorchTitan, which brings together PyTorch’s distributed and compilation capabilities for large-scale training, and Hugging Face Transformers, which provides access to community model implementations, pretrained checkpoints, and APIs for adapting models to their applications.

TorchTitan Example

TorchTitan is PyTorch’s native library for rapid experimentation and large-scale training. Its modular design makes it easier to customize training, test new ideas, and scale up experiments. TorchTitan trains on Trainium today. We continuously upstream into mainline TorchTitan, and torchtitan-neuron gives you those improvements before they merge, converging on mainline as each one lands. The Trainium-specific artifacts also ship in torchtitan-neuron and register through TorchTitan’s own extension points; those include NKI kernels, Trainium-tuned model configurations and training recipes, and profiling integrations for Neuron Explorer.

# Install from source

git clone https://github.com/aws-neuron/torchtitan-neuron
cd torchtitan
pip install -r requirements.txt

# Download the llama3-8B tokenizer

python scripts/download_hf_assets.py --repo_id meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B --assets tokenizer --hf_token=...

# Train Llama3-8B with Simple FSDP + torch.compile on a single trn2.48xlarge instance:

export NEURON_RT_NUM_CORES=64
torchrun --nnodes 1 --nproc_per_node $NEURON_RT_NUM_CORES \
--local-ranks-filter 0 --role rank --tee 3 \
--rdzv_backend c10d --rdzv_endpoint "localhost:0" \
-m torchtitan.train --module torchtitan_neuron.experiments.graph_trainer.llama3 --config simple_fsdp_llama3_8b \
--parallelism.tensor-parallel-degree 4 \
--parallelism.data-parallel-shard-degree -1 \
--training.global-batch-size 16 \
--training.local-batch-size 1 \
--compile.enable --compile.backend neuron

Following is example loss curve of training Llama 3 8B on 8 x trn2.48xlarge with Tensor Parallel (TP) and Hybrid Sharded Data Parallel (HSDP) with TorchTitan

Hugging Face Transformers v5

Transformers v5 is built for interoperability: one model implementation that runs on any platform and any hardware, and that downstream training and serving stacks consume directly.

Trainium is a supported device upstream in the Hugging Face libraries, including Transformers, Diffusers, trl and kernels. Transformers v5 enables training and inference of text and audio models, Diffusers supports image and video generation, trl enables reinforcement learning of large language models, and NKI kernels are available through the Hugging Face kernels library. AWS and Hugging Face added the support to each library, so existing Hugging Face workflows run on Trainium with no device-specific code.

  • Training. Transformers v5 strengthens full pre-training and fine-tuning readiness, with better initialization and compatibility with the parallelism and tooling ecosystem — TorchTitan for scale, Unsloth and TRL for post-training.
  • Inference. Transformers v5 standardizes attention and kernels across model implementations.
  • Diffusion. Tensor parallelism in Diffusers is merged upstream for Neuron, so image and video generation run through the diffusers APIs unchanged.
  • Compatibility. Transformers v5 is a native backend of runtime libraries such as TorchTitan, vLLM and SGLang, extending their model breadth to most of the 3 million public models available on Hugging Face. We are working on enabling and validating this integration on Neuron, bringing this expanded model support to Trainium instances.

Loading a model onto Trainium

from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B",
    # Neuron hardware is automatically detected
    device_map="neuron"
)

TorchNeuron registers Trainium through PyTorch’s PrivateUse1 extension point, which puts Neuron in PyTorch’s device enumeration. device_map=”auto” finds it with no configuration, and device_map=”neuron” names it explicitly. Either way the weights load onto the device for training or inference, and the rest of the script is unchanged.

Testing methodology and results

Our testing methodology included verifying TorchNeuron on broad model coverage across HuggingFace and TorchTitan models, and PyTorch upstream test suite across both eager and torch.compile mode.

Model coverage

Blind Sweep (Broad testing at scale). We used the Hugging Face model universe to perform broad sweep across open source models. We continuously run 100k Hugging Face models that cover 99.9% of real-world usage (based on the download count). We ran each model on Trainium in a reduced but representative configuration and record what happens: does it load, does the forward and backward pass run, does it compile, and which operators executed on the device versus fell back to CPU.

The following graph shows the result of 100k model run across eager and torch.compile mode as of September, 2026. We are working on closing the remaining gaps, targeting closing most, if not all, in future releases.

PyTorch Upstream tests

We run the PyTorch upstream test suites: ATen, Dynamo, distributed, and profiler, and report the pass rate against the enabled tests. The August 2026 run produced about 154K test outcomes, of which roughly 69K were skipped with a valid reason: About 30K of those are skipped by PyTorch own eligibility checks (for example CUDA-only and CPU-only tests) and are not Neuron-specific. The remaining ~39K are deliberate Neuron skips, in three groups

  • Operators without a native Neuron lowering at this point (~22K, the largest group; ties to operator coverage above that we plan to close in sequential releases) – corner cases for elementwise, reduction, foreach, advanced-indexing, and advanced-linalg operators, and fused LSTM/GRU cells.
  • CUDA-specific tests (i.e. the upstream eligibility check did not flag) – CUDA graphs, NCCL-specific collectives, CUDA-specific Dynamo paths tests are skipped with eligibility check.
  • Features TorchNeuron explicitly chose not to support in the first release as customers didn’t request them: composite-operator compliance, sparse tensors and sparse ops, NestedTensor, forward-mode autograd (JVP), arbitrary attention masks in native multi-head attention (no-mask and causal are supported), per-channel quantization, negative/conjugate view bits, torch.signal windows, bilinear/bicubic up sample, and dynamic and symbolic shapes.

As part of this process, we also contributed back to PyTorch by raising several RFCs and PRs to improve test quality and removing hard coded CUDA assumptions (193439, 193441, 193442, see Appendix A for complete PR list).

How to get started

Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install with pip install torch-neuronx from the AWS Neuron pip repo details.

Resources

The following resources will go live on Oct. 20:

  • TorchNeuron: https://github.com/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx
  • AWS Trainium: https://aws.amazon.com/machine-learning/trainium/
  • AWS Neuron SDK: https://aws.amazon.com/machine-learning/neuron/
  • Neuron Documentation: https://awsdocs-neuron.readthedocs-hosted.com/

Quick Reference

For further guidance on getting started, execution modes, and distributed training, see the TorchNeuron documentation.

item.dc:creator: Josh Wills, Maximilian Böther, Ties Robroek and the Zephon team

item.content:encoded:
Why Zephon?

The data that a model sees during training is one of the most powerful levers we have for influencing how well it performs. Much of the day-to-day work of improving a model happens on the data side: we change the mixture, or the filters that we apply, or how we tokenize and pack the samples, and then we run an ablation experiment to see whether the change helped. The first problem with this is that each of these changes often requires us to do a full pass over our training corpus and run expensive offline operations to prepare the data and store it on disk before our ablation experiment can run. Since a typical training run reads through that copy exactly once, and because most experiments don’t end up producing a better model, we spend a lot of time and storage creating datasets that will never be read again.

This matters even more now that experiments can be designed, launched, and interpreted by agents instead of people. Agents are great for running lots of experiments in parallel, but they aren’t especially good at noticing when a result actually depends on something other than the change they made, like the number of GPUs that an experiment happened to run on (in fairness to the agents, humans aren’t great at noticing this either). And with most data loaders, the number of GPUs does change the result, because it changes the data order.

To illustrate this, we train a 1B-parameter model in TorchTitan on 16 GPUs, take a checkpoint at step 150, and then resume from that checkpoint on 8, 32, and 64 GPUs alongside the original run, once with a standard data loader and once with Zephon (think of it as the run hitting a hardware fault and coming back on whatever set of GPUs happened to be free). As seen in Figure 1, with the standard data loader, changing the GPU count means that the data loader hands the model a different sequence of samples after the resume, and so each one ends up with a distinct loss curve. With Zephon, the curves lie on top of each other, and the SHA-256 hash of every global batch matches the baseline run.

[Figure 1: Loss curves after resuming on 8, 32, and 64 GPUs from a 16-GPU checkpoint at step 150, standard loader vs. Zephon, with a barcode comparing the per-step SHA-256 of each global batch against the original run.] 

To get a sense for how much this matters, we train the same 1B-parameter model from scratch for 20B tokens on 8, 16, 32, and 64 GPUs using a standard data loader. We show the scores per GPU count in Figure 2. The model’s DCLM Core v1 score varies by up to 0.82 points depending on how many GPUs it was trained on, and its score based on the FineWeb evaluation suite by up to 0.64 points. That is roughly four times the relevant thresholds that the DCLM and FineWeb authors used when evaluating data curation methods, which means that an ablation comparing two mixtures on two different allocations could easily be measuring the GPU count instead of the data. With Zephon, the spread across the different GPU counts was only 0.05 and 0.011 points, respectively.

[Figure 2: Downstream evaluations at 8–64 GPUs on DCLM Core v1 and FineWeb with non-elastically deterministic (standard) data loading and Zephon. Grey bands mark the eval noise floor.]

Note that Zephon does all of this while doing the data prep work on the fly: it tokenizes, packs, shuffles, and mixes the data inside of the training job, taking advantage of all of those CPUs sitting around with nothing to do while the model trains, which means there’s no preprocessed copy of the corpus to create (or to throw away when the experiment doesn’t pan out).

A Zephon Pipeline

Zephon asks you to describe three things: the Datasets you want to train on, a WorkSource that decides how those datasets are mixed and ordered into a training curriculum, and a Pipeline of operators that turn the samples in their stored representations into the tensors your training loop consumes. Here’s an example that mixes two text datasets directly from Hugging Face, then tokenizes, packs, shuffles, and batches the result: 

from zephon import Pipeline
from zephon.io import Dataset
from zephon.work import StaticMixtureWorkSource, TokenEstimation

source = StaticMixtureWorkSource(
    datasets=[
        Dataset.from_path("wiki", "hf://Salesforce/wikitext/wikitext-2-raw-v1/train"),
        Dataset.from_path("news", "hf://fancyzhx/ag_news/default/train"),
    ],
    mixture={"wiki": 0.5, "news": 0.5},   # a token ratio, not a sample ratio
    token_estimation=TokenEstimation(),
    seed=42,
)
pipeline = (
    Pipeline(source)
    .options(io_options={"cache": {"enabled": True}})
    .tokenize(tokenizer_id="gpt2", field="text", parallelism=4)
    .pack_flat(max_length=2048, algorithm="wrap")
    .shuffle(buffer_size=1024, seed=42)
    .batch(microbatch_size=8)
)
for batch in pipeline:
    train_step(batch.to_training())

The WorkSource plans the curriculum from each Dataset’s metadata and is kept separate from the operators that actually process those samples so you can change the mixture without touching the processing pipeline and vice-versa. In order to ensure we get the mixture percentages correct on a token basis, we include a TokenEstimation utility that measures the token/byte ratio for a small sample of each dataset and adjusts the plan to target the mixing proportions on a token-level even though the samples are stored as raw strings.

Each of the individual Pipeline operators can have its own level of parallelism; here, tokenization gets four workers because it’s the most expensive step. Parallelizing the preprocessing operators is how Zephon keeps the GPUs fed, even on more complex pipelines: on a full vision-language pipeline that decodes images, tokenizes, packs, and batches its samples, Zephon keeps pace with Google Grain, the fastest loader we tested, while offering the stronger elastic determinism guarantees.

[Figure 3: Usable (non-padding) tokens per second per GPU on a full vision-language pipeline as parallelism increases, for Zephon, Grain, and a quickly hacked-together internal loader we used internally before building Zephon. The horizontal line is the throughput needed to keep the GPUs from stalling.]

How Zephon Keeps the Batches Identical

Packing and mixing data on the fly is what makes elastic determinism hard. When a data loader tokenizes documents, packs them together into fixed-length sequences, and mixes several datasets together as it goes, the order of the training data is no longer something that you can look up at an index on disk (we call this stateful n:m pipelines in our paper). In this case, it depends on the state of the pipeline when and how a sample is used, and in most data loaders that state can’t be transferred to a different number of GPUs without changing the output. Existing loaders get part of the way there: Mosaic Streaming and Google Grain can keep the global batches the same across GPU counts, but only when the order of samples can be worked out ahead of time from an index, which rules out things like packing on the fly. Megatron-Energon can reproduce its batches on a different number of GPUs, but only as long as the total number of data loader workers across all of the GPUs stays the same. 

Zephon allows for elastic determinism without these constraints with three design decisions that build on each other.

Accumulators make the decisions; workers do the work. Every Zephon operator is split into two parts: a single-threaded accumulator that sees every record in order and makes all of the stateful decisions (like which sequences get packed together), and a stateless function that does the expensive work across however many parallel workers you give it. Since the workers can finish in any order, Zephon numbers each group of records before handing it out and puts the results back in order before passing them along. Unlike other data loaders, this allows that in Zephon the degree of parallelism is a pure performance knob: you can double the number of tokenization workers and the output won’t change.

Lanes instead of ranks. Instead of dividing the data up among the available GPUs directly, Zephon divides it into a fixed number of logical streams that are called lanes. Each lane has its own ordered sequence of samples and its own copy of any state that the operators need to keep (like the partially filled bins inside of a packing operator), so a lane produces exactly the same records regardless of which GPU ends up being assigned to it. When the number of data-parallel ranks changes, Zephon simply redistributes the lanes across the ranks, and the global batches come out the same. Accumulators make each lane deterministic; the lanes make Zephon elastically deterministic. The catch (you knew there had to be one) is that you need to choose the number of lanes up front, which we’ll come back to below.

Flushing and replaying instead of saving state. A Zephon checkpoint doesn’t contain the contents of any packing bins or shuffle buffers; it only records which chunks of the input were still being worked on when the checkpoint was taken. In order to keep that list short, Zephon periodically sends a flush sentinel through the pipeline that tells every stateful operator to emit whatever it’s holding and start over from a clean slate. When we restore from a checkpoint, Zephon replays the input from the most recent flush (which rebuilds the operators’ state exactly) and throws away anything the training loop has already consumed, which keeps checkpoints small (a few MiB in our experiments) no matter how far into the run you are.

Plugging Into TorchTitan

Our TorchTitan integration replaces TorchTitan’s default data loader with a Zephon Pipeline built from a data recipe (i.e., your datasets, their mixture weights, and whatever packing, shuffling, and parallelism settings you want to use), and everything else about the training run stays the same. Zephon’s state goes into TorchTitan’s checkpoint alongside the model, and since that state covers every lane, you can resume the run on a different number of GPUs from the same checkpoint. When the run launches, the integration checks that the lanes divide evenly across the data-parallel replicas and that each optimizer step’s batch splits evenly across the lanes, so a misconfigured run fails right away instead of silently changing the data several hours in. 

The repo also comes with a quick CPU-only demo that checkpoints a data stream, resumes it on a different number of data-parallel replicas, and checks that every global step matches an uninterrupted run, along with a GPU smoke test that does the same thing with a real (albeit tiny) model. The README has the commands for running each of these, plus the setup instructions, the full set of configuration options, and some example recipes to get you started.

Things to Know Before You Start

Choose your lane count. Pick a number that’s a common multiple of the data-parallel sizes you expect to run on. If you might run on 8, 16, or 32 GPUs, 32 lanes is a cap that covers all three. Don’t go overboard though (e.g., multiple thousands when your max is 16), since every extra lane per GPU adds overhead to the checkpoint’s restore time.

Keep the recipe fixed when you resume on more/fewer ranks. The data, tokenizer, seed, mixture, context length, and global batch size all need to stay the same. Of course, you may still adjust performance settings such as parallelism.

Zephon guarantees the data, not the arithmetic. The global batches will be identical across GPU counts, and the losses will be very close, but might not be identical since floating-point reduction order in the training loop still depends on how many GPUs are sharing the work.

Looking Ahead

There are a couple of directions that we’re especially excited about. The first is GIL-free Python: Zephon allows users to pick a runner, i.e., how to parallelize the operators. One runner we implemented is a thread-based runner. On Python 3.14t, it fetches vision-language samples about 3.7x faster than Zephon’s process runner does on standard Python. We think that’s where data loading is headed, and Zephon is ready for it. The second is dynamic curricula: because the curriculum is kept separate from the processing pipeline, a WorkSource can change the mixture weights over the course of a run without touching anything downstream. We’re working on a configurable curriculum component that does exactly this while keeping the determinism guarantees that we described above.

Beyond that, we would love to hear which parts of your data pipeline you would like to move into the training job and how we can help; issues and PRs are most welcome!

item.dc:creator: PyTorch Team at Meta
item.description:
Today, Meta is releasing the weights for Muse Spark Open, the most capable US open-weights model to date. It’s available today on Hugging Face under the Muse Model License. Muse...

The post Muse Spark Is Now an Open-Weights Model appeared first on PyTorch.
item.content:encoded:
Today, Meta is releasing the weights for Muse Spark Open, the most capable US open-weights model to date. It’s available today on Hugging Face under the Muse Model License. Muse Spark Open runs optimized on the SGLang and vLLM inference engines, with optimization for NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel.

Building on our August release of Muse Spark, this open weights version has additional safety post-training to make it more robust against misuse as a standalone model without system guardrails. The result is a model that is a top open source choice for safety. Muse Spark Open is an 816B total/42B active parameter model with a context window of 1M tokens. Built for coding and agentic work, Muse Spark Open is natively multimodal and shares the same base model as Muse Spark 1.3.

Meta loves open source, and as the creators of PyTorch, we’re committed to giving back to ensure the entire ecosystem fully supports Muse Spark Open. First, we’ve integrated Helion, our exciting new PyTorch-native high-level DSL for performant and portable ML kernels, to ship high-performance operations. Additionally, TorchTitan already supports Muse Spark out of the box for supervised fine-tuning and RL in the open, and we’re excited to see how far the PyTorch community can take it!

Muse Spark Open

Muse Spark Open is a coding-optimized open-weight model. Trained specifically for agentic coding workflows, it delivers higher first-attempt accuracy, reliable tool calling, and deep codebase understanding across the repos developers actually work in. You can read more in our previous model release blog here.

Enhanced Coding Capabilities

Strong at code generation, debugging, and codebase understanding. Trained on real developer workflows — multi-file refactors, debugging sessions, and long-running tasks — so the model keeps up with how you actually work. 1M context window means it handles your entire project including complex dependencies, legacy code, and thousands of files without needing to break your task into pieces

Multimodal Understanding

Muse Spark Open has audio and audio-video perception — alongside image and document understanding. As a reasoning model, it processes image, audio, and text inputs — natively and reliably.

Agentic

Muse Spark Open is built from the ground up as an agentic model. It maps out steps, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long horizons — not just single-shot tool calls. It’s trained to browse the web (including multimodal browsing), and use an agentic harness to: spawn and coordinate subagents for decomposable work; and leverage computer use capabilities unified across desktop, mobile, and browser.  It’s trained on long-horizon, multi-site tasks, and generates separate commentary that lets the model state intent before acting—so you can always know what it’s doing and why.

Why Helion kernels?

Helion is a PyTorch native kernel authoring language designed for writing high-performance kernels across heterogeneous hardware platforms. Following early adoption from the open-source ecosystem, Helion became a part of the PyTorch Foundation in April 2026. Muse Spark Open ships with Helion implementations of operations such as RoPE, RMSNorm, quantization, etc., delivering 1.03 – 3.95x speedups compared to custom kernels written in hardware specific languages (e.g. NVIDIA CUDA and CuTe DSL) on NVIDIA GB300. These same kernels were directly portable for AMD, scoring similar performance improvements on AMD Mi350 with an overall 3% improvement in end-to-end throughput.

In addition, we also launched Helion megakernels for Muse Spark Open in SGLang. Written entirely in Helion, these kernels fuse multiple operations into a single persistent kernel to improve low latency inference, and can likewise be autotuned for different shapes and hardware.

Helion kernels can be further autotuned by users for broader hardware platforms and workloads – including different accelerator architectures (NVIDIA, AMD, Google TPU, etc.), quantization formats, tensor shapes, and parallelism strategies – without maintaining separate hand-tuned implementations for every configuration. Together, these capabilities make it easier to achieve portable performance while reducing the cost of developing and maintaining specialized kernels.

Post-training  with TorchTitan

TorchTitan is a PyTorch native platform designed for rapid experimentation and large-scale training of generative AI models. Starting today, TorchTitan adds a model definition for Meta’s Muse Spark Open , so developers can tune it to their needs. 

TorchTitan features native support for multi-turn SFT and LoRA out-of-the-box, as well as reinforcement learning capabilities (TitanRL) that allow users to fine-tune Muse Spark Open.

Get Started

We’re sharing this work because we want everyone to have access to the best AI models. Muse Spark Open ships with custom, auto-tunable Helion GPU kernels in SGLang, delivering 1.03–3.95× kernel-level speedups on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs and a 3% end-to-end speedup on AMD MI350. You can also customize it for your use case by leveraging PyTorch’s TorchTitan to further tune the model.

Start Building Today: https://huggingface.co/meta-models/Muse-Spark-open-816B-A42B

Muse Spark is the full size model from our model family. We previously released Muse Glimmer, a small dense model. Start using it today, with ExecuTorch.
