item.title: Bringing ExecuTorch to Arm Cortex-M CPUs
item.dc:creator: RJ Ascani (Meta), Adrian Lundell (Arm), Siddartha Pothapragada (Meta), Digant Desai (Meta), Zingo Andersen (Arm), Måns Nilsson (Arm), Erik Lundell (Arm)
item.description:
TL;DR Deploying PyTorch models on microcontrollers has historically required converting to other framework formats, maintaining separate toolchains, and debugging cross-framework numerical mismatches. ExecuTorch eliminates this conversion step entirely. The Cortex-M...

The post Bringing ExecuTorch to Arm Cortex-M CPUs appeared first on PyTorch.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR

  • Deploying PyTorch models on microcontrollers has historically required converting to other framework formats, maintaining separate toolchains, and debugging cross-framework numerical mismatches. ExecuTorch eliminates this conversion step entirely.
  • The Cortex-M backend enables PyTorch models to run directly on Arm Cortex-M CPUs with Arm CMSIS-NN acceleration. It supports all capability tiers (Scalar, DSP, and MVE/Helium) from a single workflow.
  • We benchmark four of the five models from the MLPerf Tiny suite on the Alif Ensemble E8. Each model runs in 21.5 ms or less and uses under 90 KiB of RAM on a single Cortex-M55 core.
  • For heterogeneous SoCs, the Cortex-M backend also provides the CPU execution path alongside Ethos-U NPU delegation.
  • Minimal binary footprint. The ExecuTorch core runtime is under 20 KiB of flash, and operator selective build links only the operators your model needs, so total code size scales with the model rather than the framework.

Background

Microcontrollers power billions of always-on devices: wearables, industrial sensors, voice interfaces, and smart home appliances. These devices operate under extreme constraints: often less than 1 MB of SRAM, single-digit megabytes of flash, and power budgets measured in milliwatts. Despite these limitations, there’s growing demand to run meaningful ML workloads on these platforms and the hardware is evolving to meet it. Modern Cortex-M based microcontroller units (MCUs) now include DSP & vector ISAs, large tightly-coupled memories (TCMs), and power-efficient NPUs such as the Arm Ethos-U NPU that make ML inference more practical in resource constrained devices.

Until now, deploying ML on Cortex-M meant leaving the PyTorch ecosystem. Developers had to convert models to alternative formats, maintain separate toolchains for training and deployment, and debug numerical mismatches introduced during conversion. For teams that train in PyTorch, which accounts for over 90% of the research code published at top ML conferences, this translation step adds friction to every iteration cycle.

ExecuTorch was designed to eliminate this gap. Arm MCU support has been available through the Ethos-U NPU, and the Cortex-M backend extends it to Cortex-M CPUs, so a model can run on parts with or without an accelerator. The trained PyTorch model is exported, quantized and lowered for the device within the same stack that serves models on mobile, desktop and server.

The Cortex-M Backend

The ExecuTorch Cortex-M backend replaces standard PyTorch operators with CMSIS-NN-backed custom operators through ahead-of-time compiler passes. At inference time, these operators call directly into Arm’s CMSIS-NN library, an open source collection of optimized neural network kernels for Cortex-M processors.

Key properties:

  • CMSIS-NN accelerated. Quantized operations (linear, conv, add, mul, softmax, activations, etc.) are replaced with optimized implementations that call CMSIS-NN functions and additional optimized Cortex-M implementations directly.
  • Target-aware compilation. The CPU variant (M0 through M85) and ISA tier are specified at compile time, so the correct CMSIS-NN backend is selected, eliminating runtime dispatch overhead.
  • Purpose-built quantizer. Produces INT8 quantized graphs matching the data layout requirements of CMSIS-NN kernels, using PyTorch’s PT2E quantization framework.
  • Single compiler toolchain. The Cortex-M lowering path operates directly on the ExecuTorch edge dialect, keeping the compilation pipeline simple and debuggable.

Cortex-M Capability Tiers

The backend targets the full Cortex-M spectrum:

Tier Cores Key Feature Use Case
Scalar M0, M0+, M3, M23 Standard ARM instructions Ultra-low-cost, minimal silicon
DSP M4, M7, M33, M35P SIMD multiply-accumulate Mid-range MCUs, signal processing
MVE (aka Helium) M55, M85 128-bit vector ops, beat-based execution High-performance MCU ML inference

Arm Helium technology is where the biggest performance gains are. CMSIS-NN leverages Helium’s beat-based execution model to pipeline data movement and compute, providing significant throughput gains for the depthwise and pointwise convolutions common in edge ML architectures. That said, the same workflow targets all variants. The target configuration selects the appropriate backend automatically.

ExecuTorch is Embedded Friendly

Unlike mobile or cloud environments that must accommodate varied hardware at runtime, microcontroller deployments target a fixed hardware profile. Embedded developers possess precise knowledge of their deployment target, including the exact CPU core, available ISA extensions, SRAM allocation, and flash capacity.

ExecuTorch’s ahead-of-time stack is designed to exploit this. ExecuTorch makes target-specific decisions at compile time: graph-level optimizations, memory planning, weight packing, and kernel selection are all target-aware at compile time.

Concretely, for Cortex-M this means:

  • Graph-level compute elimination. Redundant dtype conversions, quantize/dequantize pairs, and memory format transposes are removed during lowering, so only necessary compute reaches the device.
  • Quantization parameter folding. Scale and zero-point arithmetic is precomputed into integer multiplier/shift form at export, so quantized kernel inference stays entirely in fixed-point.
  • AOT weight layout transposition. Convolution weights are transposed from PyTorch’s native layout (OIHW) to CMSIS-NN’s expected format (OHWI) at export time. The permute cost is paid once during compilation and never at inference.
  • Static memory planning across heterogeneous memories. All tensor and scratch buffers are allocated and laid out ahead of time, with support for spanning multiple memory regions (e.g., TCM and SRAM). Developers can also customize placement to put latency-critical buffers in fast local memory. No heap allocator, no fragmentation, and no runtime memory management required.
  • Target-specific operator replacement. The CortexMPassManager selects CMSIS-NN kernel variants matched to your core’s ISA tier (Scalar, DSP, or MVE) at compile time, not at runtime.

Developer Workflow

import torch
from torchao.quantization.pt2e.quantize_pt2e import convert_pt2e, prepare_pt2e

from executorch.backends.cortex_m.edge_compile_config import cortex_m_edge_compile_config
from executorch.backends.cortex_m.passes.cortex_m_pass_manager import CortexMPassManager
from executorch.backends.cortex_m.quantizer.quantizer import CortexMQuantizer
from executorch.backends.cortex_m.target_config import CortexM, CortexMTargetConfig
from executorch.exir import to_edge_transform_and_lower

# 1. Export
model = MyModel().eval()
example_inputs = (torch.randn(1, 1, 49, 10),)
exported = torch.export.export(model, example_inputs)

# 2. Quantize and calibrate
quantizer = CortexMQuantizer(use_explicit_layout=True)
prepared = prepare_pt2e(exported.module(), quantizer)
for sample in calibration_data:
    prepared(sample)
quantized = convert_pt2e(prepared)

# 3. Re-export the quantized model
quantized_exported = torch.export.export(quantized, example_inputs)

# 4. Lower to Edge and apply the Cortex-M passes
pass_manager = CortexMPassManager(
    target_config=CortexMTargetConfig(cpu=CortexM.M55),
    use_explicit_layout=True,
)
edge = to_edge_transform_and_lower(
    quantized_exported,
    compile_config=cortex_m_edge_compile_config(),
    transform_passes=pass_manager,
)

# 5. Serialize for integration into firmware
et_program = edge.to_executorch()
with open("model.pte", "wb") as f:
    f.write(et_program.buffer)

The resulting .pte binary is linked into firmware alongside the ExecuTorch runtime and CMSIS-NN library, then flashed to the device. At runtime, inference executes the precompiled graph with minimal runtime overhead and no dynamic memory allocation for tensors.

Using the Cortex-M Backend Alongside Ethos-U

Many Cortex-M MCUs pair the CPU with an Arm Ethos-U NPU such as the U55, U65, or U85. ExecuTorch’s EthosUPartitioner delegates supported operations to the NPU via the Vela compiler, and operations left outside the partition run on the Cortex-M CPU within the same graph.

The Cortex-M passes run after Ethos-U partitioning and reuse the quantization parameters already in the graph. This allows a model quantized with EthosUQuantizer to use CMSIS-NN for CPU operations whose quantization, layout and shape constraints meet the Cortex-M backend requirements. Otherwise they fall back to ExecuTorch’s portable kernels, which are functional but not accelerated.

The practical benefit is that NPU operator coverage is not an all-or-nothing gate. A model with a handful of undelegated operations can ship today on mixed CPU/NPU execution, and move more of the graph onto the NPU as coverage grows.

MLPerf Tiny Benchmark Suite

We measured inference latency and memory usage across four of the five MLPerf Tiny Inference benchmark models on the Alif Ensemble E8. These benchmark models represent a set of common deep neural networks representative of TinyML workloads. The Alif E8 integrates multiple Cortex-M55 cores alongside Ethos-U55 and U85 NPUs; we measured on a single M55 high performance core running at 400 MHz, with the Ethos-U NPUs unused. ExecuTorch’s ahead-of-time memory planning means RAM usage is deterministic and bounded, with no fragmentation risk under sustained workloads. ExecuTorch’s operator selective build was used to only include those necessary for inference, creating a minimal flash footprint. All models were INT8 quantized using the CortexMQuantizer and the Alif ML Embedded Evaluation Kit was used as a test harness. These are our own measurements rather than an official MLPerf Tiny submission, so they are not directly comparable to published results on the MLCommons leaderboard.

All four models run in under 90 KiB of RAM, three of them in under 60 KiB, and the anomaly detection autoencoder in 5.2 KiB. Code footprint stays between 15 and 37 KiB because operator selective build links only the operators each model uses.

Model Task Latency (ms) Inferences per second Peak RAM (KiB) Flash (KiB)
Model Code * Total
DS-CNN Keyword Spotting 5.825 172 26.00 37.67 36.03 73.70
MobileNet v1 0.25 Visual Wake Words 21.450 47 85.15 253.07 36.03 289.10
ResNet-8 Image Classification 15.290 65 55.14 89.77 29.82 119.59
Autoencoder Anomaly Detection 1.208 828 5.20 272.03 14.97 287.00

* Code compiled with GCC 15.2.1 includes ExecuTorch core runtime (-Oz) and kernels (-O3) with logging disabled.

Demo: Real-time Person Detector

To show what the Cortex-M backend enables in practice, we deployed a µYOLO person detection model on a Renesas EK-RA8D1 board, powered by the Arm Cortex-M85. The deployment fits comfortably within MCU-class memory constraints:

  • Task: Real-time person detection
  • Model: µYOLO, pruned depthwise separable CNN backbone with linear predictor head
  • Model size: 452 KiB (INT8 .pte file)
  • Total flash: 640 KiB
  • Peak RAM: 254 KiB
  • Inference latency: 24 ms per frame inference @ 480 MHz
  • End-to-end throughput: 12.7 FPS
  • Input: 128×128 RGB camera frame

This example of resource-constrained, always-on vision on the edge supports applications such as robotics sensing, occupancy monitoring, safety systems, smart cameras, and presence-triggered devices.

Just as importantly, the example demonstrates the development workflow enabled by ExecuTorch. The model definition, training code, export flow, and embedded deployment live within the same PyTorch-based ecosystem. Intermediate representations remain executable, making it possible to compare model outputs throughout export and lowering rather than treating deployment as a black box. The resulting graphs can also be inspected with tools such as Model Explorer, while ETDump exposes per-operator execution costs for profiling on the target. Together, these tools make it possible to iterate on model architecture, accuracy, memory use, and latency while continuously checking that transformations have preserved model behaviour. Instead of exporting a model and only discovering numerical or performance regressions after deployment, developers can inspect and execute intermediate stages of the transformation pipeline.

The model definition, training and export flow are available in the ExecuTorch repository. To facilitate an easy bring-up of the demo without the need for a physical target, the in-tree application is targeted for the Corstone FVP. Board-specific bring-up for the on-device demo was based on code from the ra-fsp-examples repo, configured with the RA Smart Configurator, built using the Arm GNU Toolchain, and flashed using J-Link Flash. For measurements above, the weights of the most expensive operators were placed in DTCM, and the instruction cache was enabled. This resulted in an inference latency reduction from 191 ms to 24 ms, a nearly 8x improvement.

Getting Started

The Cortex-M backend is available today in the ExecuTorch repository:

Resource Description
Cortex-M Backend Documentation Supported operators, target configuration, and build setup
Arm Backend Examples Full example directory with setup scripts
CMSIS-ExecuTorch Project Template Docker build + Keil Studio + AVH simulation
Zephyr RTOS Integration ExecuTorch on Zephyr with CMSIS Toolbox
Raspberry Pi Pico 2 Example Cortex-M33, MNIST digit classification

Platforms

Platform CPU Available via
Arm Corstone-300 FVP Cortex-M55 + Ethos-U55 In-tree examples, exercised in CI
Arm Corstone-320 FVP Cortex-M85 + Ethos-U85 In-tree examples, exercised in CI
Alif Ensemble E8 Cortex-M55 (MVE) Alif ML Embedded Evaluation Kit
Raspberry Pi Pico 2 Cortex-M33 (DSP) In-tree example
Renesas EK-RA8D1 Cortex-M85 Out-of-tree board port; in-tree demo runs on Corstone FVP

What’s Next

  • Expanded mixed-precision support. Extending A8W4 and A16W8 mixed-precision support across the full operator set.
  • Floating-point kernels. CMSIS-NN 8.0.0 introduced fp32 and fp16 MVE kernels. Exposing them via the Cortex-M backend enables non-fully quantized models to use the same lowering path without separate deployment flows.
  • Broader operator coverage. Adding support for attention operators, layer normalization, and other popular architecture patterns beyond traditional CNNs, along with CMSIS-DSP operators such as FFT so feature extraction can run as part of the graph.
  • More end-to-end examples. Voice activity detection, gesture recognition, predictive maintenance, and streaming wake word, the fifth MLPerf Tiny benchmark, which needs test infrastructure for multi-frame inference.
  • Additional hardware validation. Expanding the set of validated platforms and development kits.

We’re excited about what this unlocks for the embedded ML community. If you’re deploying ML at the edge, whether on a $1 sensor node or a Cortex-M55 running voice commands, ExecuTorch now provides a direct path from PyTorch training to on-device inference.

Learn more at ExecuTorch Documentation | ExecuTorch repo | Cortex-M Backend | ExecuTorch Discord

item.title: Extending Inductor for the IBM Spyre Accelerator
item.dc:creator: Dave Grove, Olivier Tardieu, IBM Spyre Team
item.description:
TL;DR The PyTorch-based software stack for IBM’s Spyre accelerator recently moved its torch.compile backend from sendnn, a separate compilation stack built entirely from scratch, to backend=inductor, an open-source backend built...

The post Extending Inductor for the IBM Spyre Accelerator appeared first on PyTorch.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR

The PyTorch-based software stack for IBM’s Spyre accelerator recently moved its torch.compile backend from sendnn, a separate compilation stack built entirely from scratch, to backend=inductor, an open-source backend built by extending PyTorch’s own Inductor. Most of Inductor carried over untouched. The real work concentrated in three places where Spyre’s hardware asks a fundamentally different question of the compiler than a GPU does. Inductor turned out to be exactly the right substrate for this work, and the result is a compiler roughly 7x smaller than what it replaced.

IBM designed Spyre as a clean-sheet AI accelerator for enterprise inference workloads, prioritizing power efficiency. It’s a 75-watt, PCIe-attached accelerator that requires no custom power delivery or cooling.

Spyre is a dataflow accelerator architected for the reduced-precision arithmetic of inference. It’s built from 32 small cores wired together over a ring, each with its own local 2 MB scratchpad rather than a shared cache. It moves data around in fixed-size chunks called sticks – 128 bytes, or 64 values in fp16.

Torch-spyre is the PyTorch integration that targets it, and this post is about growing torch-spyre’s compiler, on top of Inductor, into something that understands that hardware well.

Three things stood out as we made that move:

  1. We gained real leverage from Inductor – but we still needed substantial out-of-tree extensions at Inductor’s lower levels and in code generation. This wasn’t a drop-in swap. (The leverage is concrete enough to measure – see the code-size numbers in Evaluation.)
  2. Most of Inductor just worked. The effort concentrated on a small number of places where Spyre’s dataflow design diverges from the GPU-shaped assumptions built into Inductor – specifically, how Spyre moves data around, manages on-chip storage, and distributes work to cores.
  3. Inductor’s extension points made this tractable. We’re now working with the upstream PyTorch project to formalize the points we leaned on most heavily, so other out-of-tree hardware backends can benefit from the same leverage.

The rest of this post walks through the backend’s overall structure, the hardware differences that drove its design, how the compiler bridges them, and what we’ve measured so far.

Overall structure of the Spyre Inductor backend

Torch-spyre’s compiler implementation consists of two stages. The first stage uses Inductor extensions (living in the torch-spyre repository) to lower a torch.compile’d graph down to an intermediate representation called SuperDSC. The second stage uses a proprietary compiler called DeepTools to translate SuperDSC into the instructions that run on the Spyre hardware.

Everything in this post focuses on the first stage: the Inductor extensions.

The Inductor side plugs into the standard torch.compile pipeline – Dynamo traces the model, AOTAutograd partitions it, and Inductor lowers the resulting FX graph into its LoopLevelIR before generating code. Torch-spyre’s extensions augment this pipeline.

Extension point Stage What torch-spyre does there
Decompositions FX graph Spyre-specific op decompositions
Lowerings FX graph to LoopLevelIR Spyre-specific op lowerings
CustomPreSchedulingPasses LoopLevelIR The bulk of the Spyre-specific compiler: layout assignment, tiling, work division, scratchpad allocation

Torch-spyre registers a number of device-specific operation decompositions to map PyTorch operations such as layernorm to optimized sequences of primitive Spyre operations. It then registers a number of lowerings to teach Inductor about these primitive operations.

Most of the interesting work happens in CustomPreSchedulingPasses – it’s where tiling, layout assignment, work division, and scratchpad allocation actually get decided. It’s also the point that is, today, wired in via a monkey-patch on Inductor’s GraphLowering.codegen() rather than a first-class extension hook – the concrete formalization we’re pursuing with upstream, which we come back to at the end of this post.

LoopLevelIR is the right level for that work, but Inductor’s own hook there, _pre_fusion_custom_pass, comes too late: it only runs after LoopLevelIR has already been turned into SchedulerNodes, and Inductor doesn’t support rewriting the graph at scale once those nodes exist. Torch-spyre’s passes need exactly that kind of large-scale rewriting, which is why CustomPreSchedulingPasses hooks GraphLowering one step earlier – before Inductor has committed to SchedulerNodes and closed off large-scale transformation.

While these Spyre-specific extensions are the focus of this post, we leverage other torch.compile extension hooks too, for instance, to pool many on-device tensors into few memory allocations or to parse and propagate work division hints from source code to related compiler passes.

Three hardware differences that drive the design

Inductor was built against a mental model of the hardware underneath it – one shaped, understandably, by GPUs. Most of that model travels well to Spyre; three pieces of it don’t, and those three pieces account for nearly everything that had to be built out-of-tree.

Tensor layouts and sticks

Spyre doesn’t let a kernel address memory at the individual-element granularity that GPUs do. On a GPU, a kernel can request an individual element, even though the hardware may satisfy that request by fetching a larger cache line. The GPU exposes individual elements as the programming abstraction, while Spyre exposes the stick – a 128-byte aligned chunk of memory – as the fundamental unit of data movement and computation. A Spyre kernel must move data in sticks, with no equivalent path for moving an individual element on its own.

For a compiler that inherited GPU-shaped assumptions, that’s not a minor footnote. The index arithmetic Inductor uses to determine which tensor element a given loop iteration touches now has to reason in terms of sticks instead of elements. Beyond that indexing problem, sticks create additional challenges that GPU-focused compilers never had to face.

Each operation has specific constraints on how input and output tensor elements can be assembled into sticks. A pointwise op, for instance, requires all of its inputs and its output to agree on one shared stick dimension – the innermost dimension. When an op’s inputs arrive with incompatible sticks, the compiler has to insert a restickify: a data-movement op that physically reorders the tensor elements not just by permuting sticks but also reforming the sticks themselves. The restickify op is the one exception to the stick-immutability law. Finding an assignment of stick dimensions across a whole graph that minimizes the total cost of data movement is a global optimization problem.

Even once every stick constraint is satisfied, the on-device tensor layouts torch-spyre picks also determine performance. Suboptimal layouts have a direct impact on wall-clock time. On a batched matmul with all tensors already resident in device memory, changing how the input and output tensors are tiled cut kernel time by 29-69% across a range of batch sizes and shapes.

Together, these constraints turn layout into a graph-wide optimization problem – one that Inductor’s GPU backend was never designed to solve.

Scratchpad memories

The second difference has to do with memory hierarchies. Each of Spyre’s cores carries its own small local scratchpad – fast, but modest. Behind it there’s nothing but the global device memory. Nothing moves on its own: every trip from device memory into scratchpad, and every trip from scratchpad into a core’s compute engines, happens because the compiler emitted an explicit instruction to move it there. There’s no hardware-managed layer deciding on its own what’s worth keeping close – if the compiler doesn’t plan for a value to stay in scratchpad, it has to issue the instructions to write it back out to device memory and fetch it again the next time it’s needed. Workloads on Spyre are frequently memory-bound rather than compute-bound, so that round trip is very often where the time actually goes.

That’s a difference of degree from a GPU, not of kind – GPUs also have memory hierarchies, and plenty of the burden of using them well already falls on the programmer or compiler. But Spyre pushes further in the same direction with no automatic fallback at all. The compiler has to decide ahead of time when and where to move data to support the computation. That’s the job of the scratchpad-planning machinery described below.

Spyre’s per-core scratchpad and shared device memory

Core assignment

There’s a related, third difference: Spyre’s cores execute as a static dataflow machine. No GPU-style runtime scheduler balances load across streaming multiprocessors on the fly. That means the division of work across cores has to be decided at compile time too – which is the first theme below.

In GPU terminology, this means that Spyre kernels are naturally persistent kernels: the division of work is fixed a priori, but the scratchpad of each core can persist valuable data across many rounds of computation.

Key compiler phases

Spreading work across the cores

The first theme is dividing a single operation’s work across Spyre’s cores. Because Spyre runs as a static dataflow machine rather than relying on a runtime scheduler to balance load, this division has to be decided at compile time, per operation, before anything runs.

Torch-spyre’s work-division planner does this in three passes. First, a mandatory pass enforces a hard per-core limit on how much device memory a single core can address, committing the minimum splits needed to bring any oversized tensor back under that limit. Second, a cost-model pass specifically for matrix multiplications enumerates plausible ways to split the operation’s three dimensions, estimates the runtime of each, and picks the cheapest. A third pass handles everything else.

Take a matmul with a [8192, 32768] input, a [32768, 4096] weight, and a [8192, 4096] output, all fp16. Left unsplit, the input tensor’s memory span would exceed what a single core is allowed to address. So the first pass immediately commits a 2-way split along the reduction dimension. From there, the second pass estimates that a 16-way split along the output dimension is the most beneficial. The planner isn’t just picking a valid division. It’s picking one that minimizes the projected execution time.

Before/after for the worked matmul example: unsplit vs. a 2×4 slice of the full 2×16 core grid, showing how each core’s (K,N) coordinate picks out its A row-tile and B column-tile

The planner prioritizes matrix multiplications because they typically dominate the end-to-end computation time.

Splitting work across cores also splits the data those cores touch. A [1024, 2048] fp16 tensor is 4 MB – too big for any single core’s scratchpad – but split by rows across four cores, each core’s slice is a comfortably-sized 1 MB.

A 4 MB tensor split by rows across four cores so each core’s slice fits in scratchpad

Multi-core scratchpad residency isn’t free, though. It depends on every operation touching that tensor or tile (a buffer) agreeing on how it’s split – and nothing so far has guaranteed that agreement.

Scratchpad planning

The second theme picks up once that division of work is in place. Intermediate tensors too large for a core’s local scratchpad force a choice. Either round-trip them through device memory, or reorganize a sequence of ops to work on tensor tiles, and wrap such sequences with loops iterating over tiles. Whether tiling belongs to PyTorch or specialized programming languages such as Triton and Helion is an open question. While building torch-spyre, though, we observed that torch.scan is a powerful enough construct to express tiled loops, albeit somewhat awkwardly. Built on top of torch.scan, torch-spyre’s own for_each_tile construct makes it easy to express tiled loops, giving the programmer control about the space-time trade-off – iteration count vs. memory footprint – for instance by tiling the reduction dimension of a matrix multiplication.

for_each_tile tiling the reduction dimension of a split-K matmul, so only one K-slice of each operand is ever resident at once

Once a kernel has been tiled and tiles have been assigned to cores, the scratchpad allocator decides what actually stays resident in the core’s scratchpad and at what address. It offers a choice of solvers, from a simple greedy algorithm up to CP-SAT and simulated-annealing options for harder cases.

ScratchpadAllocator’s pass pipeline, with a pluggable choice of layout solver

The payoff is measurable. Torch-spyre’s documentation walks through a single-core softmax over a modestly sized fp16 tensor – the lowered sequence is max → sub → exp → sum → div – and shows what happens as scratchpad-aware scheduling is added one capability at a time: first pinning small reduction outputs on-core, then reusing scratchpad addresses in place for pointwise steps, then cloning the input into scratchpad once instead of re-fetching it from device memory for every reader. End to end, median kernel runtime on this example drops from 32.51 µs to 23.67 µs — a 27% reduction, purely from deciding what stays on-chip and when.

Four stages of scratchpad-aware scheduling for a softmax kernel, with total device-memory traffic per stage in units of the tensor size, from device-memory-only to fully optimized

When the two decisions fight each other

Scratchpad allocation and work division are described above as two separate passes, and torch-spyre’s first implementation ran them that way: work division picked each operation’s core split independently, and scratchpad allocation placed buffers afterward, treating those splits as fixed. That turned out to be limiting, which is why torch-spyre is moving toward the co-optimization approach described in detail below.

The problem shows up whenever two adjacent operations that share a buffer pick different core splits. Work division optimizes each operation on its own terms: a matmul wants the split that keeps its compute engines busy; a neighboring reduction or pointwise op wants whatever split matches its own shape. Nothing forces those choices to agree. When they don’t, the buffer between them is sliced differently by its producer than by its consumer – one core’s scratchpad has a piece of the data, the next op expects a different piece. Torch-spyre calls this a work-division mismatch. Historically the only way to handle it was to disqualify the buffer from scratchpad residency outright: the producer writes it out to device memory, and the consumer reads it back from there, paying for the round trip in both directions – exactly the traffic scratchpad allocation intends to avoid.

Cost of a work-division mismatch: matching splits keep a buffer on scratchpad for free, mismatched splits spill it to device memory twice over

Next, torch-spyre explored a promising alternative: decide optimal work division for each matrix multiplication in isolation but derive work division for intermediate ops from the preceding matrix multiplication, hence the decoupling of the second and third work-division passes. Device memory round trips remained the fallback when mismatches could not be avoided.

That’s no longer the only option. Spyre’s scratchpad hardware supports a core-to-core relayout – a shuffle that moves data directly from one core’s scratchpad slice to another’s, without ever touching device memory. Torch-spyre has begun turning that capability on under the name lx_relayout. A relayout doesn’t make a mismatch free: reshuffling data between cores still costs real time. And because the old layout and the new one have to coexist in scratchpad while the shuffle happens, it costs scratchpad space too. What it changes is the shape of the choice. A mismatch used to mean an all-or-nothing fallback to device memory; now it can instead mean a reasonably priced, on-chip shuffle, and the compiler gets to decide.

A better shuffle is still a shuffle, though. There is another option: moving from independent work division decisions to coordinated decisions accurately accounting for both the benefits and drawbacks of consistent scratchpad allocation across adjacent ops. Torch-spyre’s new co-optimizing allocator folds the standalone work-division pass into scratchpad planning instead of treating its output as fixed. This allocator compares the data shuffle cost resulting from optimal but mismatched work division decisions across adjacent ops to the cost of aligned but suboptimal work division decisions.

In the end, the co-optimizer has many decisions to make and many options to consider; two solver backends do that search differently. The pruned, greedy path narrows the space with hardware-specific heuristics – for a matmul, anchoring on the divisions its own cost-model pass already favors – and then places buffers with best-fit packing, keeping the search fast enough for every graph. An exhaustive constraint-programming path (torch-spyre uses OR-Tools CP-SAT) instead considers the full space of candidate divisions and relayout choices in one pass: which candidate division each operation takes, and whether any given producer-consumer pair pays for a relayout between them, tied together by hard constraints – does a buffer’s chosen division match every consumer’s, directly or via a paid-for relayout; does everything actually fit in scratchpad, including both copies while a relayout is live – with a cost to minimize once those constraints are satisfied. That relayout cost is a plain term built from the same hardware-fitted cost model that prices ordinary device-memory traffic, so the solver is never comparing a real cost against an assumed-free one. The exhaustive path can afford to fully subsume work division precisely because it isn’t pruning; the greedy path still needs the cost-model pass’s heuristics to keep its own search tractable.

The co-optimizing allocator folding work division into scratchpad planning, with a pruned greedy path and an exhaustive constraint-solver path

The payoff shows up concretely on real kernels. On a fused MLP-style kernel, letting a pointwise operation adopt a neighboring matmul’s core split – rather than insisting on its own locally optimal one – lifted core utilization from roughly two-thirds to about 80% and cut kernel time by around 17%. That translates into roughly a 2x improvement over the equivalent sendnn-compiled kernel.

On a multi-head-attention kernel, two matmuls around a softmax contract along different axes, so they can never simply adopt each other’s split outright. Offering both of them – and the softmax reduction sitting between them – a shared batch-and-output-dimension tiling let the whole chain converge on one consistent division. That pinned what would otherwise have been a device-memory round trip for the attention scores matrix.

And on a small synthetic graph built specifically to put work division and scratchpad placement in tension, letting the solver choose a relayout instead of forcing a spill replaced an 80 microsecond device-memory round trip with a 1.1 microsecond on-chip shuffle. The old strict-match gate would have paid 70x more than the problem actually required.

This is still a young part of the compiler. The search space grows quickly with the kernel size. The exhaustive solver considers that whole space. Therefore, we bound its execution time, and continue to explore smart pruning heuristics that accelerate the search for solutions without jeopardizing quality.

Evaluation

The software-engineering case for this move is easiest to see in raw size. sendnn, the compilation stack that this Inductor backend replaced, was built independently of torch-spyre and of Inductor alike. Measured with lizard (non-comment lines of code, tests excluded), it totals roughly 273,000 lines of C++ and Python across 6,170 functions, with an average per-function cyclomatic complexity around 10. The Inductor extension that replaces it, living under torch_spyre/_inductor, comes in at roughly 38,600 lines of Python across 1,878 functions, averaging a cyclomatic complexity of 5.6 per function: about 7x fewer lines, a third as many functions, and simpler ones at that.

That’s not quite an apples-to-apples “we wrote less code to do the same thing from scratch” comparison, since the Inductor extension leans on all of Inductor’s own machinery underneath it in a way sendnn never could. But that asymmetry is the point: a 7x smaller, less complex codebase is what “real leverage from an existing compiler” looks like in practice.

On performance, the fuller story is still being assembled, but two real, measured data points show up at opposite ends of the memory hierarchy. On-core, the softmax example above gives us a 27% drop in median kernel time purely from better use of scratchpad. Off-core, the matmul layout example gives us a 29-69% cut in kernel time purely from how tiling determines whether sticks land contiguously in device memory. Neither number depends on the other. Together they’re evidence that Spyre’s unique architecture poses real demands on the compiler, and that Inductor and torch-spyre can successfully tackle this challenge.

Wrapping up

Torch-spyre’s move to backend=inductor bought real leverage: a compiler roughly 7x smaller than what it replaced, and measurably less complex per function. That’s despite the fact that bridging three specific hardware gaps – stick-granularity data movement, a scratchpad-only memory hierarchy with no shared cache, a static core allocation – took substantial work outside Inductor’s own tree. What made that work tractable at all is that Inductor exposes extension points that let a backend like torch-spyre plug in without forking the compiler underneath it.

That relationship runs in both directions. Torch-spyre’s need to register device-specific decompositions – a concrete requirement that fell out of adapting Inductor to Spyre’s op set – helped drive improvements to out-of-tree Inductor backend support that landed upstream in PyTorch 2.12. We proposed the change as an RFC, and it shipped as two merged PRs: #176811 and #185909. Two design documents describing further extension points that torch-spyre relies on are also public – one proposing a tiled-layout abstraction for stick-granularity memory, one on a new MLIR-based intermediate representation (KTIR) – and we’ve already shared and discussed them with upstream Inductor maintainers: RFC 0047 – tiled tensors, RFC 0682 – KTIR. And the extension point most central to this post, CustomPreSchedulingPasses, is next in line. Turning it from today’s monkey-patch into a supported hook is an active, ongoing conversation with upstream.

We think torch-spyre is a useful proof point that Inductor’s extension-point model generalizes well beyond GPU-shaped hardware. If you’re building an out-of-tree backend for hardware that doesn’t look like a GPU, we’d like to hear from you – and, together with upstream, we’re working to make the path we took easier to follow next time.

The post Session-Aware Agentic Inference with NVIDIA Dynamo appeared first on PyTorch.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR

Agentic workloads change the traffic an inference server sees. Unlike single-turn chat, an agent session can involve a large initial prefill, repeated model calls, and subagents running in parallel, with KV cache remaining resident while tools execute between turns.

This technical blog post details how NVIDIA Dynamo uses a unified, session level identifier to transform request-level serving infrastructure into a program-aware system, unlocking session-aware routing, shared KV cache indexing, and programmatic cache movement across vLLM and SGLang.

Introduction

Agentic workloads have changed the shape of the traffic an inference server sees. A coding session opens with a large prefill, often tens of thousands of tokens of system prompt, tool definitions, and user-specific guidance, and every turn after that appends to a context the session resends in full. One task fans out into dozens of such calls, alongside short and long lived subagents running in parallel. Most of a session’s wall-clock time passes between tool calls, with its context sitting resident in the KV cache while nothing generates. Serving these well comes down to how much of that context a system keeps resident and reuses, and how many sessions it holds at once while still meeting latency targets This contrast between agentic workloads and that of a standard chatbot is shown in Figure one.

Figure 1: Compares the alternating user and model turns of a standard chatbot with an agentic workflow that includes tool calls and tool responses. In the agentic workflow, a single user request can trigger multiple inference calls, with subsequent steps depending on intermediate results.

Most open-source serving stacks are still built for the model on top of the figure. They route, admit, and cache each request on its own, with no notion of the harness or the session that ties it to previous turns.

Serving this shape optimally is something we have been building towards. In our previous post, Full-Stack Optimizations for Agentic Inference, we shared work across three layers of the NVIDIA Dynamo stack: the router, the inference engine, and the KV cache manager. Over the last few months we’ve unified this work around a single primitive: a common session-level identifier. Session-level ID (often called program or trajectory in papers and academia) turns request-aware infrastructure into program-aware infrastructure, and serves as the foundation for additional session-aware optimizations.

This post covers that progress in four parts:

  1. Session_ID: How Dynamo recognizes sessions and subagents from existing harness headers, and how custom harnesses can provide the same information.
  2. Tracing and replay: How session-linked traces connect harness activity to inference performance and support offline simulation and live benchmarking.
  3. Session-aware scheduling: How routing and admission control account for session working sets and apply backpressure at tool boundaries to reduce cache thrashing.
  4. Shared KV cache awareness: How the experimental shared-pool indexer lets the router account for reusable KV in external stores when placing requests.
  5. Programmatic KV cache: How the Session-Prefix Indexer and proposed KvHint interface support session-aware cache policies across memory tiers, with Dynamo supplying policy intent and inference engines controlling execution.

Identify Agent Sessions with Session ID

A Dynamo session ID is a unique stable identifier for a single agentic chain of reasoning and tool calls. Every LLM request in a given trajectory shares the same session_id. Usually, child sessions carry a parent_session_id, so traces and replay tools can establish a connection between agents and subagents or subtasks they spawn. Every optimization in this post is an opt-in consumer of the session information contained in session ID and parent session ID

There are a few different ways to share a stable session identifier with Dynamo, depending on what’s calling it.

Out-of-the-box support for coding agents

Dynamo recognizes the identity headers that today’s popular coding agents already emit and maps each onto the same internal agent_context: the session header becomes session_id, and the parent header, where present, becomes parent_session_id. Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode work without configuration.

Coding agent Session header Parent header
Claude Code x-claude-code-session-id (root), x-claude-code-agent-id (child agents) x-claude-code-parent-agent-id
Codex thread-id x-codex-parent-thread-id
OpenCode x-opencode-session-id x-opencode-parent-session-id

We’re working with harness providers across the ecosystem to make this the default everywhere, so support expands without users changing anything. Dynamo’s CI tracks each first-class harness as it changes. You can find a full list of supported first class IDs here.

Plugins for harnesses that don’t send session identity natively

For harnesses that don’t emit a compatible header on their own, the agent-plugins repo provides small integrations that translate a harness’s native session identity into x-dynamo-session-id. Three are available today: a Pi provider for Dynamo’s OpenAI-compatible endpoint, a Hermes middleware that maps Hermes’s session_id, and an OpenClaw provider that maps OpenClaw’s sessionId. Each plugin ships its own install, configuration, and validation steps in its own folder in the repo.

Custom harnesses: opt in with one header

A custom harness opts in with one canonical header, X-Dynamo-Session-ID. Dynamo normalizes it into an internal agent_context struct that the rest of the stack reads, so nothing downstream needs to know which harness the request came from. If the harness supports subagents, you can also provide X-Dynamo-Parent-Session-ID. The following code block shows how any custom agent can pick up Dynamo’s optimizations without adopting a proprietary API.

curl http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-dummy' \
  -H 'x-dynamo-session-id: research-run-42:researcher' \
  -d '{"model":"my-model","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"..."}]}'

Harness Inference Codesign

Agent observability tools can already capture what happens at the harness level, but they don’t yet show a unified picture of how the inference stack performed underneath each of those steps. We think about this gap as harness inference codesign: giving both sides a shared, measurable trace of the same request that can be used for performance visualization, replay, and offline simulation, all keyed by a constant session ID. This trace is meant to be lightweight. It can be used as additional optional metadata alongside other trace collection formats, like Harbor’s ATIF or Letta’s new Trajectory format.

Capturing request traces

To enable trace collection, run your deployment with DYN_REQUEST_TRACE=1. Dynamo automatically records information on each request, without storing prompt, response, or tool-call content by default (these can be opt-in enabled). Instead, Dynamo emits a request_end record after each response stream finishes, carrying the session fields, the output token count, the finish reason, KV cache metrics, tool-call names, and a replay block with the request’s input length and per-block sequence hashes, similar to the Mooncake trace format. The sequence hashes can be used for replay with tools like the built-in dynamo.replay or our load-gen tool, AIPerf.

Figure 2: Shows a screen capture of the dynamo trace, with separate tracks for agents and their tool calls. Prefill, decode, and tool execution appear on the same timeline, showing how work is sequenced and overlaps across the session.

Because every record carries timestamps and finish reasons, we can see tool-call distributions and connect them to KV cache eviction behavior. Internally, we’ve used these techniques to optimize our model deployments end to end, using captured traces as backtesting data. Much of this data and these replay tools also power our internal autoresearch harnesses, which let AI generate novel routing strategies and research proactive KV cache offloading strategies, which we cover below.

Replaying agentic traces

A captured trace is a reusable benchmark. Because it records the workload the agent sent rather than the agent’s decisions, one capture replays the same request schedule as many times as you want without rerunning the model, the tools, or any external API. Replay stays content-free the same way the trace does: sequence hashes become synthetic block IDs that preserve prompt-prefix sharing across turns and sessions without exposing the original tokens.

One capture drives two paths. Offline, AISimulate runs the request graph against Dynamo’s simulated scheduler, router, and KV cache, letting you compare worker counts, serving topologies, routing policies, and cache capacity without spending GPU time. Live, AIPerf replays the same graph against a real Dynamo endpoint on real GPUs for final latency, throughput, and cache numbers.

Routing and admission control at the session layer

KV cache has always mattered for efficient LLM inference, but agentic inference adds real complexity: where the cache lives, how much of it can be reused at each memory tier, and whether the system is proactive about prioritization, eviction, and sharing. Throughput ends up being determined less by raw compute and more by how well the stack answers those questions.

Because the Dynamo router is flexible enough to act on more than just the next request, we’ve been able to iterate on session-aware routing and admission control strategies that target these characteristics directly, improving performance for serving agentic-shaped workloads (including RL post-training). The goal is to reuse as much KV cache as possible and avoid thrashing: evicting and re-prefilling for every request because HBM, and eventually DRAM, can’t hold every agent’s working set at once.

The problem with request-level routing

A request-level router, Dynamo’s stock KvRouter included, solves placement one request at a time: given a prompt, which worker has the most cache overlap. That’s the right unit for a single turn, but it’s the wrong unit for an agent, and at high concurrency it misses two things about the agent behind the request:

  • Cache-occupancy blowup. Between turns, an agent’s cache doesn’t get freed. It sits in HBM holding blocks while the agent runs a tool call outside the GPU. With N agents concurrently at step k, the aggregate working set is N × context_k, and a request-level router has no notion of that aggregate. It only ever sees one turn’s context at a time. Once the working set exceeds HBM, and then DRAM, the engine starts evicting live sessions’ cache, and every next turn pays a full re-prefill instead of a cache hit.
  • No tool-boundary backpressure. When a worker is over capacity, a request-level router’s only levers are to cancel or queue in-flight requests. Both are worse than the alternative: deferring the session at the pause point right before its next turn arrives, when it’s about to be idle anyway.

Session Aware admission control

Our first agent-aware routing strategy ports the scheduler from the ThunderAgent paper (Kang et al., 2026) on top of Dynamo’s KV-aware router. Written in Rust, it owns a KvRouter directly rather than sitting in front of one as an extra proxy hop, and it tracks real prompt_tokens + completion_tokens off each response instead of estimating token counts from raw bytes. Because this is written as a native Dynamo plugin, you can take its source code and adapt it to your workload shape without changing Dynamo’s underlying router code.

The scheduler groups requests by program_id (the session ID) and moves each program through two independent states: (REASONING | ACTING) × (ACTIVE | PAUSED). A program enters ACTING at a tool boundary. Under memory pressure, the scheduler pauses ACTING programs logically. There’s no decode preemption; the in-flight turn is allowed to finish, which frees the engine to evict their KV blocks. If a worker has no ACTING programs left to pause, it instead marks the smallest REASONING program for pause at its next tool boundary. When a worker has headroom again, the scheduler resumes the smallest-token paused programs first, bin-packing them back under threshold.

The control loop

Pause and resume are both driven off one quantity per worker: utilization, the fraction of a worker’s KV pool occupied by its assigned programs’ working sets:

U_worker = (sum of token weights for ACTING programs on worker) / (worker's KV pool capacity)

Three thresholds (defaults shown) turn that number into a control loop:

  • U ≥ 0.95 (pause-threshold): the worker is over-subscribed. The tick pauses the smallest ACTING programs first until U falls back to 0.80 (pause-target).
  • 0.80 ≤ U < 0.95 (soft-demote band): programs aren’t paused yet, but take a -2.0 priority penalty as early backpressure before a hard pause is needed.
  • Resume only fires once U ≤ 0.85: that’s pause-threshold minus a 0.10 resume-hysteresis, a buffer below the pause line that keeps the loop from flapping between pausing and resuming right at the threshold.

Resume itself is a bin-packing pass: paused programs are sorted by token count ascending, and the scheduler admits them smallest-first until the next one would push utilization back over threshold, accounting for a fixed per-program buffer. Resumed requests get a one-second priority boost so they don’t get stuck behind fresh admissions, and a 30-minute forced-resume cap guarantees no program starves indefinitely.

Results

At moderate to high concurrency, we see a large increase in throughput. the difference shows up directly in throughput. On SWE-bench, running two TP4 MiniMax-M2 replicas on a single 8xH100 node, program-aware scheduling improved throughput roughly 12-16% over KV-routing alone, with the gap coming from the re-prefill work that request-level routing can’t avoid.

The same strategy shows a similarly large boost on agentic RL rollouts. Running Uni-Agent SWE-Bench on 8xH20-3e with Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct against VERL’s default Global LB, our strategy stayed roughly even at low concurrency (CC32-128), where nothing needed to pause. At medium concurrency (CC192-256) it pulled ahead, with 11.0-14.6% higher model-token throughput than Global LB, and at high concurrency (CC384-512) Global LB throughput dropped sharply while our strategy kept scaling. Across the full sweep it held prefix-cache hit rate above 94.5%.

Figure 3: Compares model-token throughput across agent admission concurrency levels for VERL Global LB, Dynamo Python TA, and Dynamo’s native session-aware scheduler. At high concurrency, the native scheduler maintains the highest throughput of the three, while Global LB throughput drops sharply.

Shared KV cache awareness in the router

KV cache placement gets harder once our working set outgrows HBM. The cache doesn’t disappear, it moves into CPU memory and then into shared stores like Mooncake or NIXL backed storage. So far the Dynamo router was only aware of GPU and native framework CPU offloaded memory. When KV moved into an external store, Dynamo was unable to factor it into the cost function itself. To solve this, we worked with the Mooncake team to enable KV event emission natively from the Mooncake Store and implemented a new experimental shared-pool indexer that works in conjunction with Dynamo’s blazing fast FlashIndexer. When KV is moved from HiCache (SGLang’s native CPU offloading mechanism) into Mooncake, a removal event is emitted from SGLang, and a store event is emitted from Mooncake. A page only counts as a hit when every physical object for the worker’s parallelism layout is present, and credit applies beyond its device-local prefix.

At request time, Dynamo hashes the prompt into SGLang KV pages and expands each logical page into the physical Mooncake objects implied by the worker’s TP/PP layout, K/V tensors, and optional backend tag. Mooncake publishes ordered Store and Remove events and Dynamo consumes them into a global shared-pool index, conservatively treating a page as reusable only when every required physical object is present. The index returns shared hits as contiguous page ranges rather than probing Mooncake on the routing hot path. FlashIndexer independently computes each candidate worker’s native device, CPU, and disk prefix overlap. For a worker with device-resident prefix depth D, the router credits only shared hits at positions >= D: shared_beyond_device = |shared_hit_ranges ∩ [D, request_pages)|. That prevents a GPU-local hit from being counted twice, while allowing a worker with a shorter local prefix to receive credit for the suffix already available in Mooncake. The final placement score combines weighted native-tier overlap, configurable shared-pool credit, and live worker load.

Towards Programmatic KV Cache

Ultimately, performant inference on agentic workloads requires session-aware KV block management. To predict the priority value of a given KV cache block in such workloads, we need complementary information from the router and the engine. The router is aware of session lifecycle and reuse patterns across workers; the engine is individually aware of the KV cache status it holds. Hence, for engines (vLLM, SGLang) to execute a maximally informed cache policy, (1) Dynamo should express policy intent, and (2) the engine should resolve that intent against exact cache state and execute it.

This is the central idea of programmatic KV cache. Essentially, the Dynamo router provides the “brain” that calculates smart, session/load/cache-aware KV movement policies, while the engine “executes” the movements that Dynamo mandates. As such, we have been developing features for both Dynamo and vLLM/SGLang: the machinery for Dynamo to calculate+emit KV policies, and the first-class abstractions in the engines required to lower Dynamo’s session-based policies into concrete, in-engine KV movements.

Router-Driven KV Hints Policy

Dynamo’s programmatic KV cache movements are driven by a narrow, router-initiated hint surface (”KvHint”) which enables Dynamo to pass KV cache intent to vLLM/SGLang. This avoids invasive changes to the engine’s native scheduler and cache manager. (SGLang design, vLLM design).

The orchestrator holds what a request-local policy cannot see. Which sessions are still live, which token ranges are a shared prefix versus a unique tail, whether a tool-call gap will last milliseconds or minutes, when a subagent opens and closes. That knowledge belongs in the router layer, where the harness contract and the session lifecycle already live, and it should stay there. The engine’s job is to expose the mechanism and let the router supply the intent.

The proposal is a narrow set of soft hints the router can emit to the engine. Here is a partial taxonomy of potential KvHints and their functions:

KvHint name Functionality Example use
Share Moves a cached prefix from one worker to another via p2p transfer A new engine worker warms its cache from the existing workers’ cache.
Prefetch Fetches KV from a higher tier (e.g. DRAM) to lower tier, ahead of need Reloading a main agent’s context into HBM as a subagent approaches completion.
Demote Pushes KV from a lower tier to a higher tier. Long tool call, or paused trajectory.
Pin Pins a high-value KV cache onto its current tier for a bounded TTL Pinning a system cache shared by all requests.
Retain Biases KV blocks to be more (or less) likely to be retained under cache pressure. Retaining a subagent’s KV blocks during a tool call.

Each hint carries the session ID with it, so the tier receiving the KV knows which session it belongs to and can group, place, and reclaim it as a unit rather than as anonymous blocks. That matters most in the colder tiers, where a storage backend holding host memory or disk otherwise sees only opaque hashes and has no way to tell a live trajectory’s prefix from a finished one. The engine can clip, defer, or ignore any hint, and workloads that send no hints behave exactly as they do today.

Share already has a working implementation layered into HiCache with minimal scheduler hooks, and Prefetch and Demote are designed to build on that machinery once Share lands.

Enabling KV Hint Policy Computations with Session-Prefix Indexer

For Dynamo to compose and execute these KvHint policies on the session level, it must own a continuously updated structure which bidirectionally maps between KV blocks, their session identities, and their in-session positional lineage. For this, we implemented the Session-Prefix Indexer, a radix tree structure for which each branch represents a unique session (or subagent session which branched from another).

The Session-Prefix Indexer is continuously hydrated from both inference engine KV events (Stored / Removed) and the prefix cache hits from Dynamo router’s main indexer (“FlashIndexer”). Consequently, through the FlashIndexer and Session-Prefix Indexer, the Dynamo router has a cumulative view of (1) inference engine workers’ block ownership as well as (2) those same blocks’ session membership. This information-rich view can be consumed by various KV hint policies that require signals on KV blocks’ worker location, active session lifecycles, and/or engine workloads.

With these indexers, we are actively experimenting with KvHint policies with Dynamo vLLM/SGLang on agentic workload datasets.

Figure 4: The Session-Prefix Indexer tracks shared prefixes, session lineage, and KV block locations within the Dynamo router. KV events from inference workers update this view, supporting routing decisions and policies that send optional KV hints to vLLM or SGLang.

Looking forward

Efficient agentic inference depends on managing context across the full session lifecycle. Dynamo’s session ID connects harness behavior to routing, admission control, and cache management, giving the serving stack a shared view of an agent’s evolving working set.

Session-linked traces and replay make policies measurable, while session-aware admission control reduces cache thrashing by applying backpressure at tool boundaries. In the SWE-bench configuration tested here, program-aware scheduling improved throughput by roughly 12–16% over KV-aware routing alone. The experimental shared-pool indexer extends routing visibility to external KV stores.

The Session-Prefix Indexer and proposed KvHint interface build toward proactive cache movement: Dynamo supplies policy intent, and engines retain control over execution. The key takeaway is that cache reuse and session concurrency must be optimized together. Keeping useful context available across turns and avoiding repeated prefill as concurrency grows are central to serving more agent sessions efficiently.
